en: Salutations to Viṣṇu, who is distinguished by all finite and infinite entities without exception, who reclines upon Śeṣa, and who is a treasury of stainless and infinite auspiciousness.

(1) The Supreme Brahman itself, when enveloped by ignorance and beset by delusion, wanders through the cycle of existence; embraced by external adjuncts, it becomes helpless and a locus for inauspiciousness. (2)
Victorious is that Sage of Yamunā, by whom this delusive darkness—devoid of the authority of the Vedas and logic, yet spread throughout the world—has been dispelled.

(2) This truth has been established at the summit of the multitude of Śruti texts which teach for the welfare of the entire world: that the meditation upon, worship of, and prostration before the pair of feet of the Supreme Person, preceded by knowledge of the true nature of the individual soul and the Supreme Self, and accompanied by the performance of duties according to one’s caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*), is exceedingly dear [to Him] and has His attainment as its fruit. (4)

Indeed, the collection of Vedānta texts is engaged in making known the experience of Brahman—an unsurpassed, infinite bliss—preceded by the manifestation of the true nature of the self; this [manifestation] occurs through the worship of the Supreme Self, His true nature, and the true nature of the self which is distinct from the body, along with the knowledge of the self's own nature and its intermediate states. This is for the purpose of destroying the unavoidable fear of worldly existence (*bhava*) produced by the various identifications resulting from the entry into the four types of bodies—namely those of gods such as Brahmā, humans, animals, and immovable beings—which are caused by the continuous flow of karma in the form of merit and demerit accumulated through beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*).
"That thou art.
"This Self is Brahman.
He who dwells in the self, yet is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body is the self, who controls the self from within—he is your self, the inner controller, the immortal.
This is Nārāyaṇa, the inner self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the one God.
Brahmins seek to know him through the recitation of the Vedas, through sacrifice, through charity, through austerity, and through fasting.
The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme.
"Knowing Him thus, one becomes immortal here; no other path for reaching [the goal] exists," and so forth.

(5) The true nature of the individual self (*jīvātman*) is devoid of the various distinctions consisting of specific transformations of *prakṛti* such as gods and humans; its sole qualities are knowledge and bliss.
When the distinctions such as "god" produced by karma are destroyed, the distinction of its own essential nature—which is beyond the reach of words and is to be personally realized—is [revealed].
Only this much should be indicated: that its nature is knowledge (*jñānasvarūpa*).
And that is common to all selves.
It is the sole cause for the production, maintenance, dissolution, and the administration of saṃsāra of such a manifold world (*prapañca*) consisting of both consciousness and the unconscious.

Furthermore, by virtue of being the opposite of all that is to be abandoned and possessing infinite auspiciousness, the Lord Nārāyaṇa—the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama)—is the inner controller (antaryāmin). His essential nature is distinct from all other things, his multitude of auspicious qualities is infinitely superior and innumerable, and he is known through various terms such as the Self of All, the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Light, the Supreme Reality, and the True Being, as taught by the entirety of the Vedānta. This is the nature of the inner controller.

And the Śruti texts, intent upon demonstrating His majesty, establish His governance of all things through His being the inner self of the entire aggregate of conscious and unconscious entities other than Himself; they do so by means of such terms as "His power," "a portion of Him," "His manifestation," "His nature," "His body," and "His form," as well as through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with those very terms. (7)

Regarding these terms—such as grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and others—which are intended to demonstrate its majesty, some who have set out to explain them maintain that Brahman is merely non-dual knowledge (*nirviśeṣa-jñāna-mātra*).

They hold that although it is by nature eternally liberated and self-luminous, it is nonetheless identical with the individual soul (*jīva*) as understood through the coreferentiality of such statements as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*); thus, it is Brahman itself that, when ignorant, is bound and becomes liberated.
The entire world, which consists of infinite conceptual constructs such as the Lord and the objects of his lordship, is false, being nothing other than non-differentiated pure consciousness; thus,
no such state exists as "someone is bound" or "someone is liberated."
The claim that some were liberated prior to this is false;
there is only one body possessed of life, while all others are devoid of life— why then has that single body not remained fixed?

They explain that the teacher who instructs in knowledge is false, the scripture is false, the knower of the scripture is false, and the knowledge produced by the scripture is false— all of this is understood through a scripture that is itself false. (8) Others, however, [hold that] even Brahman, though endowed with all auspicious qualities such as freedom from sin and so forth, [is realized] through this very awakening to identity.
Some maintain that [the soul] is bound and liberated when connected with a particular limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), and that it is the locus for various transformations into the form of impurities.

Others, however, describing the true nature as the realization of unity, hold that Brahman alone— which is an ocean of natural, unsurpassed, immeasurable, and sublime qualities— is by its very nature distinct from the sentient beings among gods, humans, animals, plants, hell-beings, celestial denizens, and those seeking liberation.

Furthermore, they object that [Brahman] is non-distinct [from the world] yet serves as the locus for the transformation into various impure forms such as ether and so forth. Regarding this, those intent on investigating the meaning of the Śruti cite insurmountable defects against the first position: "The word 'That' refers to the subject under discussion; it is understood that the arising, subsistence, and dissolution of the world are brought about by its own volition; thus, 'It thought'... (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6).

Beginning with the words, "May I be many, may I procreate," and continuing through such phrases as, "O gentle one, all these creatures have Being as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support," there are described— by virtue of their connection thereto—

a multitude of infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable auspicious qualities, such as omniscience, omnipotence, universal lordship, being the source of all forms, the absence of any equal or superior, the possession of true desires, the possession of true resolves, and the illumination of all things; these are indicated in other contexts [of the scriptures].

Furthermore, the state of being free from all defects, as understood from numerous passages such as "free from evil" (*apahatapāpman*), would be contradicted in that [dualistic] view. (11) Now, it might be argued that even at the outset, by means of the statement that through the knowledge of one thing everything is known, the reality of the cause alone was asserted;
and having shown the reality of that very Brahman which is the cause and the unreality of the collection of transformations by means of the analogy of clay, [the text proceeds].

By the negation of all distinctions—whether of the same class or of a different class—through the statement, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second," it is established that Brahman, which is indeed the Truth, is devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣa*).
Other passages from different sections that serve as purifiers of this [truth] are also: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite."
Passages such as "partless, actionless, devoid of qualities," and "consciousness, bliss," and so forth, make known the state of having a single form that is opposed to all specific distinctions.
Furthermore, there is no synonymy among these words in their making known this single form.
"Because even though the entity is one, all words possess meaning by establishing the exclusion (*pratyanīkatā*) of all particularities"—
this is not so.
The "knowledge of all through the knowledge of one" will not be established if everything is false, because there would be no object to be known.

Or else, there would follow the consequence of the identity of truth and falsity. Rather, the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one is established only by the fact that everything has that [one] as its self-nature. (13) This is the meaning: [the Upaniṣad] says to Śvetaketu, "You are conceited; have you asked about that instruction?"—you appear as if complete [in your knowledge], yet you have not asked those teachers about that very instruction.
That by which something is commanded is an *ādeśa*;
an *ādeśa* is an instruction.
This is because [the term] has the same meaning as [passages] such as, "O Gārgī, by this Imperishable, the sun and moon stand held apart."
And likewise, there is the statement of Manu beginning with "the ruler of all," and so forth.

Here too, by first establishing that "there is only one" as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world, and then excluding any other presiding agent (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*) through the word "without a second" (*advitīya*), it is established that this very [One] is also the presiding agent.

Therefore, you have questioned about Him who is both the presiding agent and the material cause of the world—Him by hearing, thinking, and knowing whom the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known; and by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known.

It might be said: "Have you not even heard of that Brahman, who is the cause of the origin, sustenance, and dissolution of the entire world, and who is an ocean of an immeasurable and vast multitude of qualities such as omniscience, the fulfillment of true desires, and the realization of true resolves"—
this is the underlying intention.
Since He is the cause of everything, the cause itself, when existing in various specific forms, is called the "effect";
thus, by the knowledge of Brahman—who has as His body the subtle sentient and insentient entities that constitute the cause—the entire world, which is the effect, becomes known.
Keeping this in mind, [the scripture says]: "By which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known..."
Thinking, "Let it be known," the father questioned his son.

Not understanding that this single causality of the entire collection of things was what was intended in the father's heart, the son—perceiving that it is impossible to know one thing through the knowledge of another among mutually distinct objects—questions him: "How?"
"Now, O Blessed One, what is that instruction?
Thus questioned once more, [the Lord] spoke again of that very same [Brahman], whose singular nature is knowledge, bliss, and stainless purity; whose majesty is immeasurable;
who is endowed with an infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable multitude of auspicious qualities, including the power of true resolve; and whose essential nature is immutable.

The Supreme Brahman alone, whose body consists of subtle sentient and insentient entities incapable of being divided into name and form, has established itself through its own portion as the structure of the infinite, diverse, and manifold world of moving and non-moving beings by its own will for the sake of its own sport.
(15) By declaring that through the knowledge of That, there is the knowledge of this entire universe, [the author] demonstrates the non-difference between cause and effect as perceived in the world.

He provides an illustration: "Just as, my dear, by means of a single clod of clay, all that is made of clay would be known—the modification being a mere verbal handle, a name, while the reality is simply 'clay'.
A single substance, clay, undergoes modifications in the form of various shapes and states, such as jars and bowls, so as to become the basis for various worldly transactions through its own parts.
Even though there are various names, because they are particular configurations of clay, they are simply the substance of clay existing in such a state and not some other entity.
The meaning is that, just as by the cognition of a lump of clay, everything—such as a jar, a bowl, and so forth—which consists of those particular configurations, becomes known.
(16) Therefore, not knowing that the entire world has Brahman as its sole cause, the son asks: "May your lordship indeed tell that to me."
Then, teaching that Brahman alone—omniscient and omnipotent—is the cause of all, he said: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second.
Here, by the word "this," the world is indicated;
and by "in the beginning," the time prior to creation is meant.

At that time, having established that the world consists of Being (*sat*) by means of the proposition "it is Being alone," and considering that this remains unchanged even at the time of its creation, he establishes that the world—which has attained the state of Being—is then undifferentiated in name and form (*avibhakta-nāmarūpa*).
By that very demonstration, it is established that Being is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of the world; thus, there is no efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) distinct from itself.
This was negated by the term "without a second.

In the passage beginning, "Ask about that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard," it was already established in the heart that the very Prajāpati is the material cause of the world; this is now made manifest.
Being himself both the material cause and the efficient cause of the world, he reflected: "May I become many; may I procreate."

That very Supreme Brahman, denoted by the word "That," which is omniscient, omnipotent, of true resolve, and has attained all desires, yet having willed by itself for the sake of sport—"May I indeed become many; for that purpose, may I be born"—in the form of this diverse and infinite world consisting of a mixture of consciousness and unconsciousness, created the elements beginning with space from a mere portion of its own self; and then, that same [Brahman] denoted by the word "Being" (sat) [re-entered them].
The supreme deity thought thus: "Well, let me enter these three deities with this living self (jīva-ātman) and differentiate names and forms.

By the phrase "with this living self," [the text] establishes that the living self has Brahman as its essence; it further demonstrates that it is precisely through the entry of the living self—which is identical with Brahman—that the entire non-sentient substance acquires the status of a distinct entity, and that it is only such a thing that receives a name.
This is what is meant: the individual soul (jīvātman), being a mode (prakāra) by virtue of being the body of Brahman, is essentially Brahman;
for there is another scriptural text stating, "He whose self is the body.
Thus, all things such as gods, humans, and so forth—which exist as bodies and are therefore modes of such a soul—are essentially Brahman.

Therefore, all words well-known in the world as denotative through the combination of roots and suffixes— such as "god," "human," "rākṣasa," "beast," "wild animal," "bird," "tree," "creeper," "wood," "stone," "grass," "jar," and "cloth"— are expressive only of the entire complex beginning with the object perceived in its respective form, and extending up to the individual soul identifying with it and the Supreme Self dwelling within it. (18)

Thus, having established in detail— through such passages as "All these creatures, my dear, have Being as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support"— that the entire manifold universe, consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious, has Being as its material cause, its efficient cause, its substratum, its controller, and its ultimate end; and having further demonstrated, by way of the relationship between cause and effect and so forth, that this whole world is identical with That, being "That, this is the Truth" (tatsatyam).

Having established that the world's nature as Brahman alone is the truth, [the text] declares that He alone is the Self of the entire world and the entire world is His body; therefore, even that which is denoted by the word "thou" is Brahman itself in the form of the individual soul.
Thus, the identity of everything with Brahman was proposed, and it is concluded with reference to a specific individual soul in the words, "That thou art. (19)
This is what is meant:
having pointed out that "all this is of this nature"—meaning all this manifold world of the sentient and the insentient—He has established that "this is the Self of that manifold world";
the meaning is that, by referring to the manifold world, the fact that Brahman is its very self is established.
Now, this identity with Brahman must be examined: does it exist by way of the relationship of body and self, or by way of essential nature?

If it were by way of essential nature, then the qualities of Brahman such as "truthful resolve" (satyasaṅkalpa) and so forth—understood from the opening passage, "It thought: May I be many, may I procreate"—would be contradicted. Furthermore, that identity exists by way of the relationship of body and self, as is specifically understood from another scriptural text: "He has entered within."

The Teacher is the "Self of all people" because, by virtue of being the Ruler, He has entered within all people as their very Self; thus, He is the Self of all people. Furthermore, it is specifically known that His nature is Brahman, for it is said: "He who dwells in the self, yet is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body is the self, and who controls the self from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. Regarding this point as well, it was already stated previously that by the words "by this living self," it is understood to be this very [Brahman] itself.

Therefore, since all conscious and unconscious entities constitute the body of Brahman, Brahman alone is denoted by all words in every possible manner. Thus, through the grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of "That" and "Thou," Brahman itself is denoted in its aspect as the living self (*jīva*), by virtue of being the body of the living self. (20)

When this has been stated, the following meaning is understood: that which was previously perceived as the presiding agent of the body is, in fact, a mode of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), having the Supreme Self as its body and culminating in the Supreme Self; therefore, the word "thou" (*tvam*) denotes not merely the individual soul, but specifically the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) characterized by that mode. This is because, according to the text, "Having entered with this living self (*jīva-ātman*), let me manifest names and forms," the embodied individual soul (*jīva*) is [defined] precisely by its identity with Brahman.

Because they possess their own respective denotations, both words—*tat* (That) and *tvam* (Thou)—which function in grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), must have Brahman alone as their referent.
In this context, the word *tat* denotes that very Brahman which is the cause of the universe, the source of the multitude of all auspicious qualities, faultless, and changeless.
And the word *tvam* denotes that same Brahman as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of the individual soul, characterized by the mode of having a body.
Thus, it has been explained how the two words "That" and "Thou" function with respect to the one Brahman alone through a distinction in their *pravṛttinimitta* (grounds for application).
The fact that Brahman is faultless, changeless, a mine of all collections of auspicious qualities, and the cause of the world is thereby established as uncontradicted.

(21) Persons who have not heard the Vedānta do not perceive that all categories of objects and even individual souls (*jīvātman*) are of the nature of Brahman; nor do they perceive that the denotative power of all words culminates in the complete [Brahman], rather than merely in the specific portion of the object denoted by each respective word.
They believe this:

now, by hearing the Vedānta texts, they understand that everything has Brahman as its self because it is an effect of Brahman and because Brahman is its inner controller; and they understand that all words denote Brahman as it exists in its respective modes.

[Objection: But in that case, the linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) whereby words such as "cow" denote their respective objects would be subverted. [Reply: This is not so; for it has already been stated in the passage, "Let me manifest names and forms," that all words are denotative of the Supreme Self as qualified by non-sentient matter (*acit*) and individual souls (*jīva*).

In this regard, worldly persons, when uttering a word, consider that the completion of the denotation occurs within a single part of the object denoted— since the principal aspect, the Supreme Self, cannot be delimited by perception and other means of knowledge—
whereas through the hearing of the Vedānta, their proficiency [in understanding] is fulfilled.
In this very way, all Vedic words convey their own meanings as culminating in the Supreme Self.

All Vedic words indeed were extracted one by one from the Veda by the Supreme Brahman himself; having created all objects as before, he employed them as names—as they had been before—for those objects ending with the Supreme Self.
Regarding this, Manu says: "In the beginning, he fashioned the individual names and actions of all beings, as well as their distinct social orders, from the very words of the Veda."
Thus, "configurations" (saṃsthāḥ) means shapes (saṃsthānāni), that is to say, forms (rūpāṇi).
And the Blessed One Parāśara said: "Name and form are the manifestation of beings and their activities."
In the beginning, he composed the [treatises] on the gods and other subjects from the very words of the Vedas.
Thus [it is said]. And the Śruti says: "The Creator fashioned the sun and the moon as before.
The meaning is that, having fashioned the sun and the others as they were previously, He established their names as they were before.
In this way, the non-difference between the world and Brahman has been elaborated.
By means of that single instance of knowledge, the knowledge of everything is established.
By demonstrating that everything has Brahman as its effect, its reality is shown to consist solely in its having that [Brahman] as its essence, and not otherwise; thus it is said, "That is the Truth.
Just as in the illustration, everything that is a modification of clay has reality only by virtue of having clay as its essence. (23)
The purificatory statements (*śodhakavākya*) also reveal the Supreme Brahman as irreproachable and the source of all auspicious qualities.

Even when they teach that [Brahman] possesses the nature of being the opposite of everything else, since differentiation is unavoidable regarding those various contrary natures, there is no establishment of a featureless reality.
(24) But surely, once it is established that Brahman is mere consciousness (*jñānamātra*), it is determined that Brahman is mere consciousness devoid of distinctions.
It is not so;
for words that have the nature of defining their own form (svarūpa) convey the form itself by way of its properties (dharma),
just like the word "cow" and others.

Regarding this, the author of the Sūtras says: "Because its essence consists of those qualities, it is designated by them, as in the case of the Wise One (Prājña); and because it is permeated by the Self, there is no fault. Thus, by means of the attribute of knowledge, its own nature is also defined; Brahman is not mere knowledge alone.

If it is asked how this is understood, [the answer is: this is established by hundreds of scriptural passages such as "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving," which testify to His nature as a knower; "His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold, and His knowledge, strength, and action are innate"; and "By what, my dear, should one know the Knower? Furthermore, since knowledge is merely an attribute (*dharma*), it is logically untenable for a single attribute alone to be established as the ultimate reality.
Therefore, words such as "satya" (truth) and "jñāna" (knowledge) denote Brahman itself as qualified by knowledge and the other attributes that constitute their own primary meanings.

However, if both words in the phrase "tat tvam asi" (That thou art) were to abandon their own primary meanings in order to bring about the presentation of the nature of a non-distinct reality, there would be the fault of abandoning the primary sense (*mukhyārthaparityāga*).
[Objection: But surely, because the intention (*tātparya*) is determined to be oneness, the fault of *lakṣaṇā* (indication/metaphorical transfer) does not apply.
It is like the expression "this is that Devadatta.

Just as in the phrase "this is that," by the word "that" a person connected with another place and another time is understood, and by the word "this" one connected with the present time and the immediate location is understood; through their grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), their identity is perceived.

If it is argued that, since the simultaneous cognition of a single entity as being connected to two contradictory places and times is impossible, the two words must therefore be intended merely to present the individual forms (svarūpa) of those two [places and times], and that one thereby understands the identity of the individual form— this is not so. Even in the case of "This is that Devadatta," there is not even a trace of figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).
Because there is no contradiction;
it is not contradictory for a single entity to be connected with two actions, one past and one present.
Having existed while situated in another location, it now exists while situated in a proximate location.
Therefore, the presentation of identity through the connection with two actions—one past and one present—is not contradictory.
Furthermore, the contradiction regarding two different locations is resolved by the difference in time.
Even in the case of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), there is no need to resort to figurative indication for both words.

By this very definition, since the contradiction is avoided, it is stated that there is an absence of [any] defining characteristic [of contradiction]. For there is no contradiction in that which has already come into being through its connection with one place existing as connected with another place. (26)

Thus, here too it has been established that there is no contradiction in the Supreme Brahman—which is the cause of the world—possessing the nature of the individual soul (*jīvātmatva*) by virtue of being the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) of the soul.
For grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is understood to signify the identity of two things as they actually exist;

the identity of mere essential natures (*svarūpa-mātra*), setting aside those [actual] entities, is not the meaning of coreferentiality. This is because coreferentiality is defined as the application of words with distinct grounds for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*) to a single referent.
We have already established the identity of those two [states] as they truly are.
Furthermore, it is not possible to determine the purport of a sentence based on a concluding word that contradicts its opening;
for in the opening, by such passages as "It thought: 'May I be many,'" both the possession of true resolve and the state of being the sole cause of the universe were declared.
Furthermore, qualities such as being the locus of ignorance are contrary to that [Brahman]. Moreover,

since words and sentences derive their status as valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) from their capacity to convey the distinctions between objects, the relations between them, and their specific qualifiers, and since they lack the power to convey a reality devoid of attributes, word is not a valid means of knowledge regarding a reality without attributes.

Words such as "without distinction" (*nirviśeṣa*) and so forth, however, convey their meaning by negating the distinctions belonging to another thing with respect to an object that has been understood as qualified by some particular distinction;
otherwise, they would be entirely non-informative.
This is because a word, consisting of a stem and a suffix, contains within itself multiple distinctions, and a sentence conveys the connection between the meanings of multiple words. (28)

Now, it might be argued: "We do not say that words are a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to a reality that is devoid of distinctions and self-luminous, because that which is established by itself does not depend upon a means of valid cognition. By all words, however, all specific attributes superimposed upon it—such as being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) and so forth—are excluded."
"When all particularities have ceased, the mere thing (vastumātra), being unconditioned and self-luminous, remains by itself"—
this is not so.
By what word could that thing be pointed out such that its particularities might then be excluded?
If it is argued that this is by means of the term "mere cognition" (*jñaptimātra*), we say no;
for even that relies upon an entity possessing distinctions,
since it contains distinctions within its nature as consisting of both stem and suffix.

The verbal root *jñā*, meaning "to cognize," is understood from its primary form (*prakṛti*) as a specific action that possesses an object, possesses an agent, and has a nature that distinguishes it from other actions;
furthermore, the suffix (*pratyaya*) conveys gender, number, and so forth.
Even though [the action] is self-established, its establishment would not occur at all were it devoid of these specific natures.

For the self-evident establishment of cognition is said to consist in its not having the nature of being established by any other means. (29) If the entire nature of Brahman were to manifest by itself at all times, then the superimposition of another attribute upon it would be impossible;
for when the true nature of a rope is manifest, one does not superimpose the state of being a snake or the like upon it.
For this very reason, you yourselves accept the existence of obscuring ignorance (*ācchādikā-avidyā*).
Consequently, the object of the scriptural knowledge that brings about cessation is that portion of Brahman which remains concealed; otherwise, that knowledge would lack the power of cessation.
For the nature of the snake is sublated by the manifestation of the rope-ness that transcends the locus [of the illusion].

If a single particularity is denoted by a word regarding the entity that is pure consciousness, and that [particularity] becomes a qualification of Brahman, then Brahman becomes characterized by all the qualifications propounded by all the scriptures.
Therefore, for those who rely on valid means of knowledge, the existence of a featureless entity is not established by any means of valid cognition whatsoever.
Even in non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*), an object is apprehended as possessing specific qualities;
otherwise, in the subsequent conceptual stage (*savikalpaka*), the cognition "this is that" characterized by previously understood qualifiers would be impossible.

Since universals such as "cowness" consist in the specific configuration (*saṃsthāna*) of the object, even during the state of non-conceptualization, the object is perceived as having that very configuration in this manner.
In the second and subsequent cognitions, there is perceived merely the fact that this particular configuration resides in multiple objects.

Since the category known as "configuration" (saṃsthāna-rūpa-prakāra) qualifies multiple objects by virtue of residing in them, it is understood through the second and subsequent cognitions; thus, these second and subsequent cognitions are called conceptual (savikalpaka).
For this very reason, the dual nature of a single entity in the form of being both different and non-different has been refuted as contradictory.

Since the configuration (*saṃsthāna*) is a mode (*prakāra*) of the configured object (*saṃsthānin*), it is not a separate category of entity. Precisely because it is a mode, it cannot exist independently, nor can it be perceived separately; thus, its dual nature is not established. (31)

Furthermore, by one who asserts that all words exclude specific qualities from a self-luminous reality which is devoid of distinctions, it must be stated which words are the negators. If you argue that this is what the scripture says— namely, that because modifications and names are merely "begun with speech" (*vācārambhaṇam*), that which is indicated there as the mere reality (*vastumātra*) by virtue of being the cause is alone real, while everything else is unreal— this is not tenable.
When it is asserted that "when one thing is known, everything becomes known," for one who considers the knowledge of one thing impossible through the knowledge of another, this example is shown:

if a single reality indeed exists as name and form through various specific states such as modifications and so forth—which are ultimately real—then when that one thing is known, even a different configuration distinct from it is understood to be that very same thing. Thus, this illustration is presented.
No word whatsoever is seen here that negates any particularity.
Regarding the phrase *vācārambhaṇam*: it is called "commencement" (*ārambhaṇam*) because it is commenced by speech—that is, by conventional usage.
While the clay remains as clay, its name is one thing and its conventional designation is another.
The very same clay, existing in the form of jars, bowls, and so forth, has different names and conventional designations according to its various states;

nevertheless, in all cases, the substance of clay is one and the same, which is initiated through various forms, various names, and various conventions—this alone is the truth. By this, it is demonstrated that the cognition of one thing can arise from the cognition of another.

It has already been explained previously that no entity whatsoever is being negated here. Furthermore, if the falsity of everything other than Brahman were intended to be asserted by the passage beginning with "By which the unheard becomes heard," then the illustration provided in the passage beginning with "As, my dear, by a single lump of clay" would be deficient in its probandum (*sādhyavikala*).

If it is argued that this— namely, that the unreality of transformations of clay such as jars and bowls, like a snake [superimposed] on a rope and so forth, is unestablished for Śvetaketu through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and through reasoning (*yukti*), and thus remains something yet to be proven—
then the employment of the example "just as" (*yathā*) is not appropriate. (33)

If it is argued that in the passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second," the two restrictions—"Being alone" and "one only"—along with the phrase "without a second," indicate that all distinctions whatsoever, whether of the same class or of a different class, are excluded as being other than pure Being; we reply: this is not so.

Having demonstrated through an illustration that a single entity, existing in two states as cause and effect, becomes known— even when it exists in one state— by means of knowledge of it while it exists in the other state due to the identity of the thing itself; and having stated that the fact of Brahman being the cause of all was unknown to Śvetaketu, the text begins with "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone."
"In the beginning, this was indeed Being alone.
Here, "in the beginning" (*agra*) refers to a particular time.

This [statement] expresses both the action consisting of the manifestation of the world—which is denoted by the word "this"—as having attained the state of Being, and its substantial reality as Being (*sad-dravyatā*).
And by the statement "only one," there is the abandonment of the manifold transformations of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
When this is established, it is demonstrated that this world has Being (*sat*) as its material cause (*upādāna*).
For although elsewhere the material cause is seen to require a presiding agent distinct from itself, [Being here] is entirely different [from such causes].
The phrase "without a second" excludes any other presiding agent, because it is not contradictory for this omniscient Brahman to possess all powers; indeed,

it is precisely because Brahman is endowed with all powers that certain scriptural passages, having first established its status as the material cause, further establish that it alone is also the efficient cause.
Just as this scripture—

and other scriptures as well— having first acknowledged Brahman’s status as the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), raise the objection as to how He can also be the material cause (*upādānatā*) and so forth,
they resolve it by stating that because He is endowed with all powers, Brahman alone is both the material cause and all other remaining instruments.

What was the wood, and what was that tree, from which the wise fashioned heaven and earth? Ask this in your mind: upon what did he stand while supporting the worlds? The sacred word (*brahman*) was the wood, the sacred word was that tree, from which the wise fashioned heaven and earth; I declare it to you in my mind: the sacred word stood firm while supporting the worlds.
Having raised the objection of contradiction based on the general observation that "one who maintains [the world]," a resolution was stated by means of Brahman's being distinct from everything.
Therefore, even in the passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," various specific attributes such as "in the beginning" and so forth are presented regarding Brahman;
no word whatsoever is seen there that expresses a negation of the specific attributes you favor.
On the contrary, the existence of a specific time denoted by "in the beginning" (agra) is for the purpose of making known the relationship of cause and effect between the world and Brahman;
and "was" (āsīt) is a specific verbal action.

The fact that Brahman is both the material cause (*upādāna*) and the efficient cause (*nimitta*) of the world, as well as its possession of all powers through the refutation of any distinction between the efficient and material causes—these specific points, though not explicitly stated [in the opening], have been established in thousands of ways. Precisely because [the inquiry] proceeds from the knowledge of the real relationship between cause and effect, the refutation of the theory of non-existent effects (*asatkāryavāda*) is carried out, beginning with the words, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (*asad vā idam agra āsīt*), and continuing with, "But how indeed, my dear, could it be thus? (*kutas tu khalu somyaivam*).
The word "syāt" means that the arising of what was previously non-existent would be without a cause.
He demonstrates this very point by asking: "How could the existent arise from the non-existent?"
The meaning is that what is produced from the non-existent becomes of the very nature of the non-existent;
just as a jar or the like produced from clay is of the nature of clay.
What is called "production from the existent" is the acquisition of a particular state that serves as the cause for a specific conventional designation. (35)
This is what is meant:
a single substance that serves as the cause is designated as the "effect" through its association with a different state; thus, it is intended to demonstrate that by knowing one, everything is known.
This will not be established under the theory of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*).

For instance, since an effect known as a composite whole (*avayavin*)— which is a distinct substance— is produced from causes such as the efficient cause (*nimitta*), the inherent cause (*samavāyin*), and the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyin*), it follows that because the effect is a different entity from the causal entity, it is in no way possible for the cognition of the former to result from the cognition of the latter.

If it is asked how the existence of a distinct composite substance (*avayavidravyāntara*) is refuted: [the answer is] because the very [process] accepted by those who maintain that the production of a distinct substance consists in its connection with a different state residing in the causes, is sufficient to account for such things as its unity or its change of name; and because no distinct substance is observed. Thus, it has been stated that the cause itself, having undergone a change of state, is called the "effect. (36)

[Objection: Is it not the case that the refutation of the theory of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*) is performed in order to demonstrate the impossibility of an error without a substratum? For indeed, since a single conscious reality (*cidrūpa*), though veiled by ignorance (*avidyā*), undergoes a phenomenal transformation (*vivarta*) into the form of the world, one must accept that the root cause is real in order for it to serve as the locus of ignorance; thus, the theory of the non-existence of the effect is refuted.
[Reply: This is not so.

It has been stated that because of the argument by way of example regarding the thesis that all cognitions arise from a single cognition, the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) alone follows as a consequence;
furthermore, in your position, it is difficult to establish the impossibility of an error occurring without a real substratum (*niradhiṣṭhāna*).

For one for whom the defect residing in consciousness is ultimately real and the state of being the locus of defects is ultimately real, there can be the perception of ultimately unreal things—such as a city of Gandharvas—by means of that ultimately real defect.

But for one for whom the defect is unreal and the state of being the locus of that defect is also unreal, it is possible for that [defect] to exist even with an unreal locus; thus, in your own position, there is no impossibility of an error without a substratum (*niradhiṣṭhāna-bhrama*).

Furthermore, in purificatory passages such as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite" and "Brahman is bliss," it is not contradictory to understand a single object qualified by multiple attributes, since this is established through the conventional usage of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); therefore, Brahman is denoted as qualified by all its attributes.

This has already been stated previously. (38) Now, if it is argued that a negation is observed in various ways through the instruction "not this, not this," then it must be explained what is being negated here.
If it is argued that the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), consisting of both the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*)—the two forms of Brahman—are being negated, this is not so.
It is improper to first teach everything that is not known as a form of Brahman by way of its being a form, and then subsequently negate that very thing;
for according to the maxim, "it is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off."

What, then, is the meaning of the prohibitive statement? The author of the Sūtras himself declares: "For [the text] prohibits only that which has been previously mentioned as being of such a nature; thereafter it speaks further. Since in the subsequent passage—"Now follows the name: 'The True of the True. The vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed the True; of these, He is the True"—a multitude of qualities beginning with Truth is established, it follows that what was previously mentioned as being merely of such a nature is what is prohibited.
"It does not become Brahman" means that the limitation of Brahman to such a [finite] measure is what is being negated; this is the meaning of the Sūtra.
If it is argued that the negation of plurality alone is observed in passages such as "There is no diversity whatsoever here," [we reply:]...

In this context as well, and in what follows, because it is established that [the Lord] is "the controller of all" and "the ruler of all," which demonstrates His possession of true resolve (*satya-saṅkalpatva*) and His status as the Lord of all, the Lord has a sentient being as His body; thus, He alone exists in every mode of manifestation. Consequently, the manifoldness consisting of non-Brahman—which is the opposite of that [unity]—is negated, not that which you yourself intend.
In all such scriptural passages, this same principle holds; thus, nowhere is any word found that expresses a negation of Brahman’s possession of attributes.
Furthermore, the view that Brahman is mere attributeless consciousness, and that its true nature being concealed by *avidyā*—which obscures it—it perceives an internal plurality, is untenable.
For "concealment" (*tirodhāna*) means the prevention of manifestation.

Since you do not admit the existence of any property of illumination distinct from its own nature, and because illumination is itself the very nature [of the self], there would necessarily be the destruction of that nature.
To say that "knowledge," which is a synonym for illumination, is eternal, and that this illumination is merely concealed by ignorance (*avidyā*), is the talk of a fool.
For if illumination is concealed by ignorance, it must mean either an obstruction to the arising of illumination or the destruction of that which already exists.
Since light cannot be produced, it would necessarily be subject to destruction.

If you argue that light remains eternal and immutable, then even while ignorance exists, nothing is concealed within Brahman; thus, your conventional expression that "one perceives multiplicity" is itself indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*), despite the existence [of Brahman]. (41)
But surely, even for you, the self must be admitted to have the nature of consciousness,
and that [consciousness] is self-luminous. Furthermore,
when that [self] identifies with the nature of a god or other such states, the obscuration of its own luminous nature must necessarily be accepted.

Since it is impossible for another form to be superimposed upon one's own self when its own nature is manifest, this fault is common to you as well. Furthermore, while for us this difficulty you have raised applies to only a single Self, for you—who accept the plurality of Selves—this fault must be resolved in respect to all of them. (42)

To this it is replied: [He is] by His very nature the singular essence of infinite knowledge and bliss, which is the adversary of impurity; an ocean of natural, boundless, unsurpassed, and immeasurable noble qualities;

whose infinite great manifestations are not obscured by the transformations produced by time—the cause of all arising, persistence, destruction, and all other modifications—consisting of the divisions of *nimeṣa*, *kāṣṭhā*, *kalā*, *muhūrta*, and so forth, up to the limit of *parārdha*.

The object of knowledge is the Supreme Brahman alone, who exists in the state of supreme excellence, possessing a body consisting of all powers by virtue of being the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) of the entire multitude of entities— both sentient and non-sentient— including His own play-companions (*svalīlāparikara*), the infinite bound and liberated souls who are His own portions (*svāṃśa*), and the infinite diverse objects of enjoyment for them, as well as the power of infinite manifold transformations.

For us—who accept the Veda, which consists of infinite branches in the form of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva; whose textual tradition of recitation is eternal, beginningless, endless, and uninterrupted; which is the ultimate reality; and which is augmented by the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and Dharmaśāstras, all of which have as their source the Veda in the form of injunctions, explanatory passages, and mantras composed by hosts of sages such as the Lord Dvaipāyana, Parāśara, Vālmīki, Manu, Yājñavalkya, Gautama, and Āpastamba—what will not be accomplished?
As it was said by the venerable Dvaipāyana in the Mahābhārata:
He who knows me as unborn and beginningless, the Great Lord of the worlds—
there are these two persons in the world, the perishable and the imperishable;
the perishable consists of all beings, while the one who stands firm is called the imperishable.
But the Supreme Person is another, declared as the Supreme Self—
the imperishable Lord who, having entered the three worlds, sustains them.
And there, time ripens [all things], for time has no power there;
these indeed, my dear, are the hells belonging to the abode of the Supreme Self.
From the unmanifest (avyakta) up to the specific (viśeṣa), all this is joined with the power of transformation;
let it be understood that all this is the perishable play of Hari.
For Kṛṣṇa alone is the origin and also the dissolution of the worlds;
indeed, this entire universe, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, exists for the sake of Kṛṣṇa.
Thus [it is said]: "For it is done for Kṛṣṇa" means that everything is subordinate to Kṛṣṇa.
It has also been stated by the venerable Parāśara:
"The supreme Brahman, known as the Great Sovereignty (mahāvibhūti), is designated by the word 'pure'."
O Maitreya, the word "Bhagavat" refers to the cause of all causes.
Knowledge, power, strength, sovereignty, valor, and splendor— in their entirety,
and devoid of all qualities and attributes subject to abandonment— are what is denoted by the word "Bhagavat."
In this way, O Maitreya, this great sound "Bhagavān" belongs to Vāsudeva, who has become the Supreme Brahman; it does not apply to anyone else.
In this context, this word is accompanied by a technical convention (paribhāṣā) denoting an object worthy of worship;
it is not used figuratively (upacāreṇa), for elsewhere it is indeed used figuratively.
Such is the stainless truth, all-pervading and imperishable,
devoid of all that is to be abandoned— the supreme state known as Viṣṇu.
And time, consisting of units such as *kalās* and *muhūrtas*, is not the cause of transformation for that which is His manifestation.
Behold his movements, like those of a child at play.
And so forth. Manu also said:
"The ruler of all, subtler than the subtlest.
Yājñavalkya also [said]:
"From the knowledge of the Lord of the field (kṣetrajña), supreme purity is attained.

Thus [it is said]. Āpastamba also states: "All living beings are indeed the city of the one who dwells in the cave. The meaning is that all living beings are the city, the fortress, the body of the Supreme Self who dwells in the cave.
"Living beings" (*prāṇin*) refers to the aggregate of the vital breath, the self, and the elements. Now, what is the use of this elaborate display?
The objection has not yet been resolved.

It is replied: For us who accept this— maintaining that consciousness, which constitutes the very nature of the self, though innate, undergoes ultimate contraction and expansion through the influence of karma— all of this [objection] is refuted.
Since existence (*bhava*) has manifestation (*prakāśa*) alone as its essential nature (*svarūpa*), manifestation is not a quality (*dharma*) of it, nor are contraction and expansion admitted for it.
Karma and other factors, which constitute concealment (*tirodhāna*), merely prevent the expansion of manifestation;

it has already been stated previously that if ignorance (*avidyā*) were the concealment, then by being a concealment, it would entail the destruction of the manifestation that constitutes the essential nature through that ignorance.
In our case, however, the light that constitutes our own essential, eternal nature is contracted by karma in the form of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Consequently, there arises the identification with the self as having the nature of gods and so forth; this is the distinction. As it has been said:
"Ignorance is held to be another power, distinct [from the other two], known as karma."
Just as the power of the field (kṣetra-śakti), O King, though all-pervading, is enveloped [by ignorance],
it undergoes all the continuous torments of saṃsāra.
And because it is concealed by that [māyā], O King, the power known as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) exists within all beings in varying degrees.

Thus, [the text] shows that for the knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*), there is contraction and expansion of their own inherent knowledge through the ignorance designated as "action" (*karman*). Furthermore, the concealing ignorance (*ācchādikā-avidyā*) is accepted—both by the scriptures and by the force of the teaching of non-duality—as being of the nature of a defect to be abandoned that obscures the true nature of Brahman. Since this [ignorance], being illusory in nature, depends upon a defect rooted in its own perception just like the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), it cannot itself be the defect rooted in illusory perception; rather, Brahman alone would have to be the root of illusory perception.

And although that [beginningless nature] is beginningless, because it is of a false nature and is beginningless only as an object of perception for Brahman, and because one does not admit a real defect as its root cause, Brahman itself must be the root of that perception; since Brahman is eternal, there would be no liberation at all. For this very reason, the following view is also refuted: that the single body alone possesses a living soul (*jīva*).
The other bodies are soulless, just as the various infinite bodies seen in a dream are soulless.
In that context, the body of the dreamer is the only one possessed of a soul;
all the various bodies appearing as objects of perception during the time of the dream are indeed devoid of a soul.

Because this [jīva] alone is imagined, the individual souls (jīvas) are unreal; for Brahmā has imagined the state of being a soul as distinct from His own nature, as well as all bodies. Since, even in a single body, the state of being a soul is unreal—just like the body itself—all bodies are therefore unreal in nature.
In that case, since the state of being a living being is illusory in nature, there would be no distinction whatsoever between a single body and the state of being a living being therein.

For us, however, because the dreamer’s own body and the existence of the self within it remain unsublated at the time of awakening, whereas other bodies and the living beings residing within them are sublated, all of those latter are illusory.
The distinction is that one's own body alone exists therein, and the state of being a living soul (*jīvabhāva*) is merely the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Furthermore, it must be investigated by whom ignorance (*avidyā*) is removed and what its nature is.
If it is argued that the knowledge of unity (*aikyajñāna*) is the remover and that the removal takes the form of the opposite of the indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*), [we respond as follows]:
That which is expressible is the opposite of the inexpressible; and whether it be existent, non-existent, or of a dual nature, no other alternative category exists.
If this [world] were admitted to exist apart from Brahman, then ignorance would never cease.
If Brahman itself is the cessation, then since it was indistinguishable even prior to that, cessation would have occurred even before the knowledge of Vedānta arose.

Your view—that the knowledge of unity (*aikyajñāna*) is the remover [of ignorance] and that saṃsāra exists because of its absence—is undermined. Furthermore, since even the knowledge that removes [ignorance] is of the nature of ignorance, it must be stated by what means that [removing knowledge] itself is removed.

If you argue that the removing knowledge, having removed all other distinctions, perishes of its own accord due to its momentariness—just as a forest fire or a specific antidote destroys poison—it is not so.

Since the subverting knowledge (*nivartakajñāna*) is distinct from Brahman, its own nature, its origination, and its destruction are all of the nature of falsehood; therefore, since ignorance (*avidyā*), which consists in the destruction of that [knowledge], must indeed persist, one must certainly state a further subverter for the perception of that [ignorance’s] destruction.
Even in the case of forest fires and the like, a succession of transformations that oppose their prior state is unavoidable. (48)
Furthermore, who is this knower of the knowledge whose object is the negation of everything other than Brahman, which is pure consciousness?
If you say it is of the nature of superimposition (adhyāsa), no;
for since that [superimposition] is itself what is being negated, it is the object of the subverting knowledge, and thus it is logically impossible for it to be its agent.
If it is argued that [the self] is indeed of the very nature of Brahman, we say no.
Regarding the knowledge that removes [ignorance], is the subjecthood (*jñātṛtva*) of Brahman its essential nature (*svarūpa*) or superimposed (*adhyasta*)?
If it is superimposed, then this superimposition and the other ignorance (*avidyā*) which is its root must remain precisely as the objects of the knowledge that effects removal.

If one were to accept another [cognition] as the remover of that [uncertainty], then because that too would possess the three-fold nature [of a valid means of knowledge], there would be an infinite regress.
For if any cognition lacked the three-fold nature, its very status as a cognition would be lost,
since it must consist in the establishment of some specific object for someone.

If knowledge lacks the three-fold nature [of being known, knower, and knowing], then for you, even the annulling knowledge (*nivartaka-jñāna*) would be incapable of annulment, just like the knowledge that constitutes its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).

If it is admitted that the very nature of Brahman is the knower, then your position would simply be adopting our own view. Furthermore, the statement that the knower-ship of the annulling knowledge is included within that which is to be annulled by it [is untenable], as it is distinct from the ground [upon which the object rests].

The statement "Devadatta has cut everything" is laughable, like saying that within this very act of cutting, the agent of cutting and the object to be cut are both included within that same act of cutting.
Furthermore, one must investigate by whom this knowledge of oneness— which eliminates all distinctions— was produced.
If it is argued that [the world] is sublated by scripture itself, we say no;

for since scripture, as something distinct from Brahman, is itself imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*), it is impossible for it to produce the knowledge that sublates the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).

To illustrate: even the cognition of a snake in a rope, though produced by defective causes, is not sublated by the cognition "this is a rope, not a snake," which is likewise produced by defective causes.

While the fear arising from the cognition of a snake in a rope persists, even if some deluded person says, "This is a rope, not a snake," once it is known that this person is himself deluded, his words do not sublate the cognition of the snake in the rope, and the fear does not cease.

For at the very moment of hearing [the scripture], one who possesses the prompting knowledge (prayojakajñāna) realizes that even the scripture itself is rooted in error because it is distinct from Brahman.

If it is argued that the sublater knowledge (nivartakajñāna), its knower, and the scripture— which constitutes its causal complex— are all sublated because they are distinct from Brahman, then alas, the falsity of the cessation of the phenomenal world (prapañca-nivṛtti) would follow,
and thus the reality of the phenomenal world would result.

Just as for one who has learned of the death of a father or other relative through the words of a person seen in a dream, that [dream] is false while the reality of the father and others remains; furthermore, a sentence such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) is not a sublater of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), because it is rooted in delusion, like a sentence uttered by a deluded person to counteract the [perception of] a rope-snake. (50)

But surely, when some fear is present in a dream and one realizes during that very state of dreaming, "This is a dream," the cessation of the prior fear is observed; the same could happen here as well.
It is not so.
Even when it is recognized that what occurred at the time of dreaming was itself a dream, it is observed that fear does not cease; thus, there is no distinction [between the two cases].
It has already been stated that even at the very moment of hearing [the teaching], it is understood that this too was a dream.

Furthermore, as for the claim that the scripture—though false in form because it is a conceptual construction based on error—nevertheless makes known the non-dual Brahman, since no subsequent sublation of that existent Brahman, which is its object, is ever observed...
"That Brahman is indeed well-established"—
this is incorrect,
because that [notion] too is sublated by the statement, "That Thou Art is indeed empty."
If you argue that this statement is based on error,
then you yourself have stated that even the statement "Brahman is Being, non-dual" is based on error.
The distinction, however, is that the subsequent observation of its non-sublation applies only to the statement of universal emptiness.

Furthermore, it has been established by those who are learned that proponents of universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyavādin*) and those who maintain the falsity of all entities other than Brahman have no standing in debate, because they do not accept the ultimate validity of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that establish their own positions.
As it is said: "The proponent of emptiness has no standing in debate, because [his position] lacks a means [of proof].
(52) Moreover, by what means of knowledge is the falsity of this phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), to be established?
If it is argued that because perception can be established otherwise by being rooted in defects, the faultless scripture—which cannot be established otherwise—is the sublater of perception;
then it must be stated: by what defect is perception produced such that its object consists of infinite distinctions?
If it is said that perception is produced by the defect known as the beginningless latent impression (*vāsanā*) of distinctions; [then...]

Alas, in that case, the scripture too would be produced by this very same defect; thus, because they share a common root in a single defect, the relationship of sublated and sublator between scripture and perception cannot be established.
Perception is that which grasps objects existing in the form of human beings and so forth, endowed with the elements such as space and air, and their derived qualities such as sound and touch.

The scripture, however, has as its subject matter the nature of Brahman—characterized by infinite attributes such as being the inner self of all and being the Truth—as well as the methods for propitiating it through meditation and other means, the specific fruits obtainable by its grace preceded by attaining it, and the specific forms of restraint that uproot the performance of what is undesirable.
Thus, there is no contradiction between scripture and perception.
Furthermore, scripture possesses superior authority due to its possession of numerous qualities, such as having an unbroken tradition of recitation that is without beginning or end.

Since one who speaks must necessarily accept the ultimate reality of direct perception (*pratyakṣapāramārthya*), enough of this refutation—like the winnowing away of cotton-like webs of fallacious arguments by the wind-force of hundreds of scriptural citations; thus we desist.

However, in the second alternative, because no entity other than Brahman and its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is admitted, all defects arising from the association with limiting adjuncts would belong to Brahman itself.
Consequently, all scriptural passages declaring its faultlessness, such as "free from sin" (*apahatapāpmatva*), would be contradicted. (55)

If it is argued that just as the space within a jar (*ghaṭākāśa*) and the like, due to their limited nature, are seen to differ from and be distinct from the great space (*mahākāśa*), and thus any qualities or defects residing therein do not attach to the undivided great space; likewise, the defects belonging to the individual souls (*jīva*), which are established as distinct by their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), do not attach to the supreme Brahman, which is free from such adjuncts.
This is not tenable;

for since space is partless and indivisible, it is impossible for it to be partitioned by jars and the like. Thus, just as jars and other objects would be conjoined with that very same space, so too, because Brahman is indivisible, Brahman itself would be conjoined with the limiting adjuncts (upādhis).
If it is argued that the portion of space conjoined with a jar is distinct from another portion of space, [we reply:

since space is one and the same, its conjunction with a jar or other objects occurs through a distinction of portions; thus, when the jar moves, there is no fixed rule regarding that distinction of portions.

In the same way, because of the association with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) through an unfixed distinction of portions within Brahman itself, when the adjunct moves, there arises a distinction between the portions of Brahman that are conjoined and disjoined [with the adjunct].
Furthermore, the wise mock [this view], saying that if the association with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) were to occur in Brahman alone, there would be bondage and liberation at every single moment.

If it is argued that just as the sense-organ of hearing (*śrotra*) is a partless ether (*ākāśa*), yet a specific arrangement of the senses is possible, so too an arrangement is possible for Brahman—[we reply:

no, because the sense-organ is only that portion of ether conjoined with the region of the ear refined by a particular wind; and while that [ether] does not differ from other regions, the arrangement of the senses is established.

However, while space, moving through all bodies according to its own laws, comes into contact with all locations, there is likewise no restriction regarding the locations of contact with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) in the case of Brahman. (57) Even if it were accepted that the auditory faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) is space by its very nature, the established order of the faculties would still hold;
yet, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), space is not the auditory faculty.
For the followers of the Vedas maintain that the eleven sense organs are born from the *vaikārika* (sattvic) *ahaṃkāra*;
as it was stated by the venerable Parāśara:
"They say the [five] sensory organs are *taijasa* (rajasic), while the ten deities [of action] are *vaikārika*."
"And here, the eleventh is the mind; these are remembered as the deities of the *vaikārika* [type].
This is the meaning:
ego (*ahaṃkāra*) is threefold—*vaikārika*, *taijasa*, and *bhūtādi*.

And that [ahaṃkāra] is, in sequence, sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa. Having stated the order of creation— that from the *tāmasa* *bhūtādi* the elements such as space (*ākāśa*) arise— and having introduced the view of others— that the eleven organs arise from the *rājasa* *taijasa* *ahaṃkāra*— [it is taught that] the *vaikārika* organs arise from the *sāttvika* *ahaṃkāra*.
The statement "they are born" expresses his own view, as it is said that "the gods are known as the vaikārika [forms].
The gods are the sense organs.
Thus, the nourishment (*āpyāyana*) of the sense organs—which are derived from the ego (*ahaṃkāra*)—by means of the elements is described in the Mahābhārata.
Even if the sense organs are material, since they are merely modifications of the elements such as space, they exist as specific transformations of those very elements;

thus, like bodies, the sense organs belong to persons. However, in the case of Brahman—which is indivisible, partless, and changeless—this position is one that only the faithful can accept, for the defect of an unrestricted association with infinite limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is indeed difficult to avoid.
Thus, those who know the scriptures do not hold this in high regard;
for by accepting a transformation of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), the scriptural teaching of its immutability is contradicted.
If it is argued that Brahman’s faultlessness refers to a transformation of its power (*śakti*), [the response follows].
What is this so-called power? Is it of the nature of a transformation of Brahman, or is it something else that is non-different from Brahman?

In both cases, a transformation of the essential nature (*svarūpapariṇāma*) is indeed unavoidable. Even in the third position, since one accepts both the difference and the non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, and because that [non-difference] exists as their very being, all defects residing in the individual souls would belong to Him alone— just as in the case of the various manifestations of Saubhari and just as in the case of His own incarnations, everything is a manifestation of the Lord.
This is what is meant:
it is described that Īśvara exists by his very nature as the various states of gods, humans, animals, and stationary beings;

for if that were the case, then just as all functions such as carrying water, which belong to a jar, a bowl, and so forth produced from a single lump of clay, belong to that [clay] alone, [so too would all effects belong to Īśvara].
In this way, all pleasure, pain, and so forth residing in every living being would necessarily reside in the Lord alone.

If it is argued that just as the material substance of clay—which has not yet been applied to the forms of jars, bowls, and the like—is already associated with other effects, so too the Lord, though not yet applied to the states of gods, animals, humans, and so forth, is omniscient and a mine of auspicious qualities such as the power of true resolve; [we reply: True, he is indeed that very Lord, but only in one aspect.
It has been stated that he who is a mine of a multitude of auspicious qualities is, by another aspect, a mine of qualities to be abandoned;
for there is no difference between the two aspects regarding the Lord.
If it is argued that the two aspects are established as distinct, [the response follows].
What is the benefit of that?
Since a single being is eternally suffering in one respect, its state of happiness in another respect does not suffice for it to be considered *Īśvara*.
It is just as when Devadatta has the application of sandalwood paste, armlets, bracelets, and rings as ornaments on one hand, while on his other [hand]... [he has none].

Just as there would be the blow of a mallet upon one's hand and the entry into the flames of the fire of time, so too would it be for the Lord; thus, this position of difference-and-non-difference is even more wretched than the position of Brahman-ignorance, because the immeasurable suffering [of the world] would be ultimately real and because it would be insurmountable due to the infinity of transmigrating beings. (60)
If it is argued that this individual soul (jīvāṃśa) is therefore of a different nature [from the Lord],
then you have indeed entered my own path;
for this objection would apply only if one were describing an identity with the Lord in terms of His essential nature (svarūpa).
However, there is no fault whatsoever in establishing identity by means of the relation between self and body;

on the contrary, this great collection of qualities, such as the governance of the entire universe and so forth, becomes established, and the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is taken in its primary sense. (61)
Furthermore, it has been stated that for a single entity, the state of being both different and non-different is impossible due to contradiction:
if a jar is different from a cloth, it is absent in that cloth;
if it is non-different, it is present in it.
For it is contradictory for a single entity to exist and not exist simultaneously at one time and in one place.
If it is argued that there is existence by way of its universal nature (*jāti*) and non-existence by way of its individual manifestation (*vyakti*),
then since the universal is absent in a bald man, it would follow as an absurd consequence that the universal "baldness" must also exist in a broken-horned [cow].

Furthermore, if the universal (*jāti*) is non-different from the individual (*khaṇḍa*), it would exist [in all individuals]; if it is different, it would not exist [therein], just as "cowness" does not exist in a horse. Thus, the contradiction is indeed difficult to avoid.

Since universals and the like are the structural forms (*saṃsthāna*) of things and thus constitute the modes (*prakāra*) of the thing, the mode and the bearer of the mode (*prakārin*) are distinct categories. Moreover, the mode cannot be established independently, nor is it perceived separately; and such a structural form resides in multiple things.
That it exists as a mode (*prakāra*) and so forth has been stated previously.
(63) The cognition "this is that" arises because of the identity of the mode, just like the cognition "this person also [is] one with a staff.
Furthermore, this mode—consisting of the universal (*jāti*) and so forth—is called the differentiation (*bheda*) of the entity.
The meaning is that the very connection with that [cognition] is the cause for the conventional usage "the object is distinct.
And that [connection] is the cause for the conventional usage of distinction regarding the object, as well as for its own [usage], just like self-awareness (*saṃvedana*).
For example, just as self-awareness is the cause for the conventional usage of the object and the cause for its own conventional usage, so too is this [connection]. (64)
For this very reason, arguments such as "perception grasps only pure existence and does not grasp difference" are refuted;

for it is precisely an entity established with a configuration consisting of genus and so forth that is grasped by perception, and it is that very configuration—genus and so forth—which, in dependence upon a counter-correlate, serves as the cause for the conventional usage of "difference.
Furthermore, the fault of the modification of the essential nature (*svarūpa-pariṇāma*) has already been stated previously. (65)

He who, dwelling in the earth, is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body is the earth, who controls the earth from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. He who, dwelling in the self, is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body is the self, who controls the self from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.
He who moves within the earth, whose body is the earth, whom the earth does not know—and so forth, up to—he who [dwells] in the Imperishable...

Moving within the interval, whose body is the Imperishable (akṣara), whom the Imperishable does not know; moving within the interval, whose body is Death (mṛtyu), whom Death does not know—this is the inner Self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the one God, Nārāyaṇa.
Two birds, companions and friends, closely united, perch upon the same tree.
Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit of the *pippala* tree, while the other looks on, not eating.
He has entered within as the teacher of people, the Self of all.
Having created that, he entered into it.
Having entered into that, it became both the existent and the non-existent, the unreal and the real—[as stated in the passage] beginning with "by means of this living self.
Having perceived the Self and the Impeller as distinct, one rejoices; through that, one attains immortality.
Having understood the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the impeller—all this that has been declared as the threefold Brahman—[one realizes:
"He is the eternal among the non-eternal, the consciousness among the conscious, the one who fulfills the desires of the many;
He is the Lord of Pradhāna and Kṣetrajña, the Master of the Guṇas."
"By hundreds of such scriptural passages and their corroborative texts— such as 'The two, the knower and the ignorant, the Lord and the non-Lord'—
it is established that the entire universe is Your body, and the surface of the earth is Your stability."
O twice-born one, whatever being is created by whatever means,
in the production of all that which is created, everything indeed is the body of Hari.
I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa, dwelling in the heart of all beings.
And I am seated in the heart of all; from me come memory, knowledge, and their loss.

From such words of Vālmīki, Parāśara, and Dvaipāyana— the foremost among those learned in the Vedas— it is understood that the Supreme Brahman is the Self of all; and since it is understood that the entire reality, consisting of the sentient and the insentient, has Him as its body, and because a body is a category of existence only by way of being a mode (prakāra) with respect to the embodied one, and because there is no confusion between the body and the embodied one despite their difference in attributes, Brahman is the Self of all bodies.

By means of primary modes of expression such as grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), which establish the majesty of Brahman, Brahman alone is denoted in all its forms as both sentient and insentient.
For grammatical coordination is the state of two words being directed toward a single referent by way of two distinct aspects.
And this [latter] view is primary in this context.

For instance, in the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of "That" and "Thou," by the word "That" is meant Brahman—the cause of the universe, the mine of all multitudes of auspicious qualities, and the faultless;

and by the word "Thou," functioning through coreferentiality with a conscious being, is meant Brahman as existing in the form of that [individual soul], having that as its self, and having that as its limiting adjunct (*prakāra*), specifically as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of the living being.
In the other alternative views, there would be a loss of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and Brahman would possess the quality of being an existent entity (*sattva*).
This is what is meant:
