in the statement "Brahman is situated thus," the existence of the manifold world—consisting of diverse sentient and insentient beings, both gross and subtle—is established precisely as the mode (*prakāra*) that constitutes the referent of the word "thus" (*evam*).
And thus, the meaning "May I become many; may I be born forth" is fulfilled.
For that very Lord, who exists in various configurations as both effect and cause, the entire aggregate of conscious and unconscious entities subsists by virtue of those configurations.

(67) Now, it may be objected that the referent of the word *evaṃ* (thus) is observed to be only a genus (*jāti*) or a quality (*guṇa*) when they function as modes (*prakāra*) through their formal configuration (*saṃsthāna*), but not a substance (*dravya*).

It is improper to claim that God is merely a mode (*prakāra*) of a category (*padārtha*) that is capable of being established as an independent entity (*svatantra*), on the grounds that such is the meaning of the word "thus" (*evaṃ*).
It is replied: even in the case of a substance (*dravya*), such as a staff or an earring, it is indeed observed to function as a mode of another substance.
[Objection: But surely, when an independent object like a staff functions as a mode of another substance, we observe the use of possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya-pratyaya*).

Just as one says "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*) or "the man with earrings" (*kuṇḍalin*), so too, because of the similarity to [the category of] "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth, it is not logical to establish a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) by presenting conscious and unconscious things as substances (*dravya*) as being modes of God (*īśvara*).

To this it is replied: in expressions such as "cow," "horse," "human," and "god," it is precisely substances consisting of aggregates of elements (*bhūta-saṃghāta-rūpa*) that are meant—such as when it is said, "Devadatta was born as a human through a particular merit (*puṇya-viśeṣa*)," or "Yajñadatta was born as a cow through evil."

It is observed that there is a presentation through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "the world" and "a god," such as in the statement, "Another conscious being, by means of an abundance of merit, has been born as a god," where the bodies of gods and so forth are modes of consciousness.
This is the meaning: whether it be a genus (*jāti*), a quality (*guṇa*), or a substance (*dravya*), no particular regard is paid to that [category].

For whatever exists merely as a qualifier with respect to a certain particular substance, its presentation through coreferentiality as a mode of that [substance] is logical, because of its non-separate establishment (*apṛthaksiddhi*) from it.

Furthermore, in the case of a substance that is established as distinct [from others] yet is at some time or place intended to be a mode (*prakāra*) of another substance, there is the use of a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya-pratyaya*); this is the distinction.

In exactly the same way, since every entity consisting of the stationary and the moving has its very existence (*svarūpa-sadbhāva*) solely as a mode of the Lord by virtue of being His body, it is logical to establish [the relationship] through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), because the Lord, who possesses those modes, is denoted by those respective words.
All this has already been explained in detail previously in the exposition of the scriptural passage concerning the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*).

Therefore, since the entire effect— consisting of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), the individual soul (*puruṣa*), the great principle (*mahat*), the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the gross elements (*bhūta*), the sense organs (*indriya*), the fourteen worlds (*caturdaśabhuvana*) composed of those, and all the various types of beings existing within that cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) such as gods, animals, humans, and stationary objects— is established as being of the very nature of Brahman, everything becomes known through the knowledge of Brahman alone, which is the cause.
The knowledge of all through a single knowledge is more logically established.

Thus, by way of the relationship of cause and effect and so forth, it has been stated that the entire reality—both conscious and unconscious—is of the nature of the Supreme Brahman, being its very self as its mode (*prakāra*).

(70) But surely, the status of the Supreme Brahman as the locus of transformation in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) has been refuted, on the grounds that it would contradict scriptural texts declaring its changelessness and faultlessness?

And by the sūtra, "The [world] is the material cause (prakṛti), because there is no contradiction with the initial proposition and the illustrative example," it is established that the Supreme Person is the material cause of the world through the proposition that "by the knowledge of one, all is known" and the example of clay and its products;
and being a material cause consists precisely in being the locus of transformation (pariṇāma).
How is this established?
To this it is replied: It has been stated that the world of plurality (*prapañca*) together with the living beings (*sajīva*) is the cause without distinction.

In that regard, by accepting the transformation of the Lord (*īśvara*) into the form of the living beings, there is no contradiction with the [scriptural] statements such as "the Self [is not the cause], because of the eternity [of the Self] and because of those [scriptures]."

Furthermore, the avoidance of the charges of partiality and cruelty was established by accepting that the individual soul (*jīva*) is beginningless and that [the world's diversity] is caused by its own karma—namely, that partiality and cruelty do not apply because [the Lord] is dependent on [karma], as stated in the Sūtra: "If it be argued that [He is not partial] because He is dependent [on karma] and because of the distribution of karma, we say no; because [the soul] is beginningless, and this is both logical and observed. Moreover, the consequence of the acquisition of what was not done and the loss of what was done (*akṛtābhyāgama-kṛtavipraṇāśa*) was declared in the case of [the soul's] impermanence. (72)
Likewise, the beginninglessness of *prakṛti* is established by the scriptures:
"The one unborn female, red, white, and black, producing many offspring similar to herself;
one unborn male, delighting in her, lies by her, while another unborn male leaves her after he has enjoyed her pleasures."

Thus, he demonstrates the unborn nature of both Prakṛti and Puruṣa. Furthermore, by stating, "The Illusionist creates this entire universe, and another, bound by that [Illusion], is confined within it; one should know Prakṛti as Māyā and the Great Lord as the Illusionist," he shows that Prakṛti alone, by its very nature, is the locus of transformation.
"The cow is without beginning or end; she is the mother, the bringer-forth of all beings.
And there is also a Smṛti:
"Know that both Prakṛti and Puruṣa are indeed without beginning."
And know that both the transformations and the qualities arise from Prakṛti.
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind,
intellect, and ego— thus is my nature divided eightfold.
But know that this other nature of Mine, which is distinct from this, is the supreme one— the life-force, O mighty-armed one, by which this entire world is sustained.
Taking hold of my own nature, I project forth [the world] again and again;
under my supervision, nature gives birth to the moving and the unmoving.
Thus it begins.

And in this way, since primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is also the body of the Lord (*īśvara*), the word "primordial nature" denotes the Lord who has that as his essence, or who exists in the mode of that [nature]. Likewise, the word "person" (*puruṣa*) also denotes the Lord who has that as his essence, or who exists in the mode of a person.
Therefore, for their modifications as well, the Lord alone is the Self. Thus it is said:
"The manifest is Viṣṇu, and likewise the unmanifest, the Puruṣa, and Time itself;
O Brahmin, that Supreme Lord is both the agitator and the object to be agitated."

Thus, since the Supreme Self exists as the substrate (*prakāra*) of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), there is modification (*vikāra*) in the aspect that constitutes primordial nature, while there is no modification in the aspect that constitutes the substrate itself. In exactly the same way, since the Supreme Self exists as the substrate of the individual soul (*jīva*), all that is contrary to the goals of man (*apuruṣārtha*) resides in the aspect that constitutes the individual soul; whereas the substrate-aspect is the Ruler, faultless, the source of all auspicious qualities, and truly of realized will (*satyasaṃkalpa*). (74)

This being the case, since God alone exists in the causal state, He alone also exists in the state of the world as its effect derived from that material cause; thus, there is non-difference between cause and effect, and there is no contradiction with any of the Śrutis.

Therefore, Brahman—whose body consists of Prakṛti and Puruṣa having entered a subtle state unfit for the differentiation of name and form—is the causal state, and the dissolution of the world is simply its return to that state.
Brahman, whose body consists of the gross sentient and insentient entities differentiated by the division of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), possesses the state of being an effect;
the manifestation of Brahman in such a gross form is called the creation of the world.
As it was stated by the venerable Parāśara:
"Pradhāna and Puruṣa, which are unproduced, are the cause of those things that have become effects. (75) Therefore,

words denoting primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and the individual self (*puruṣa*) in all their states— which are modes of the Lord— refer primarily to the Supreme Self as it exists distinguished by those modes,
just like the words "living being" (*jīva*) or "human" (*manuṣya*).

Just as words such as "god" and "human" primarily refer to the Supreme Self—the possessor of modes—because they denote specific transformations of the material nature (*prakṛti*) of gods and humans as modes (*prakāra*) of the individual self (*jīvātman*), so too all denotative words primarily refer to the Supreme Self. This is because every conscious and unconscious entity is a mode of the Supreme Self by virtue of being His body. And this very relationship of self and body consists of: (1) the relationship of substrate and superstratum, which is incapable of separate existence; (2) the relationship of controller and controlled; and (3) the relationship of the whole and its parts.

It is called the *ātman* because it pervades [the body] as its substratum, controller, and sovereign in every respect; and it is called the *ākāra* (form) because it is non-separately established (*apṛthaksiddha*) as the mode (*prakāra*) of being, being the supported, the controlled, and the subordinate in every respect. This is precisely how the individual soul (*jīvātman*) is related to its own body.
In this very way, because the Supreme Self is the body of all, it is denotable by all words.

Regarding this, the collection of Śruti texts says: "The word that all the Vedas declare," and "In whom all the Vedas become one. The meaning is that because that One is the object denoted, [all words] come to denote a single referent.
"The one God has entered into many forms;
though He exists together [with them], the gods do not recognize Him," and so forth.
Here, "gods" (*devāḥ*) refers to the sense faculties (*indriyāṇi*).

The meaning is that the senses, beginning with the mind, do not perceive Him who exists together with gods, humans, and others, having entered into them as their inner controller (antaryāmin) and as their very self.
And thus say the Puranic verses: "We bow to that eternal foundation of all words, in which [all speech] is established."
For the word has its foundation in that which is to be expressed;
among all effects, the cause is prior, and among words, the object to be expressed is supreme.
And by all the Vedas, I alone am to be known.
Indeed, all such statements as these refer exclusively to the Inner Controller (antaryāmī) as qualified by the embodied self;
for the Śruti declares: "Come, let me enter these three deities with this living self (jīva) and differentiate names and forms.
And likewise is the statement of Manu:
One should know that Supreme Person as the ruler of all, subtler than the subtlest, radiant like gold, and attainable through the intellect in deep sleep.

Having entered within as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*), he is the ruler and regulator of all; subtler than the subtle self because, while those various selves are subtle due to pervading the entire insentient world, he pervades even them and is therefore more subtle than they—
golden-hued, possessing the color of the sun, and attainable by an intellect resembling the state of dream.
The meaning is that He is attainable solely through meditation that has reached the state of most vivid direct perception.
Regarding Him, some call Him Agni, others Māruta, others Prajāpati; some call Him Indra, others Prāmāṇa, and still others the eternal Brahman.

Thus [it is said]. "Some Vedas" means certain Vedic texts. The meaning is that, because the Supreme Brahman alone—by virtue of being the ruler of all and having entered and remained as the inner self of everything—exists in this manner, even words such as "fire" (agni) become designators of that very [Brahman], just like the eternal word "Brahman."
And so another Smṛti says:
"Those who sacrifice to the ancestors, the gods, and the Brahmins together with the sacrificial fires,
they indeed sacrifice to Viṣṇu alone, the inner self of all beings."
Thus, it is stated that words such as "father," "god," "Brāhmaṇa," and "fire" denote Viṣṇu alone, who is the inner self within them by way of those [entities].

(78) Herein lies the heart of all the scriptures: the individual souls (*jīvātman*), though their own nature consists of uncontracted, unlimited, and pure knowledge, become enveloped by ignorance in the form of karma; they enter into various and diverse bodies ranging from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, undergoing a contraction of knowledge corresponding to each respective karma, and attain an expansion of knowledge suited to each particular body.

Those who identify with their respective bodies as the self perform actions appropriate to that state and enter the stream of saṃsāra, which consists of the experience of pleasure and pain corresponding to those actions.

Since their liberation from this saṃsāra is not possible without taking refuge in the Blessed Lord, for that purpose, [the author] first establishes the equality of all beings—free from distinctions such as gods and so forth—in their uniform nature of pure consciousness;

and having established that even that essential nature has the Blessed Lord as its sole essence by being His subordinate (śeṣa), he further demonstrates that they have the Blessed Lord as their very self (bhagavadātmakatā).

Having established that the nature of the Blessed Lord is entirely distinct from everything else—being exclusively composed of auspicious qualities that are the opposite of all that is to be abandoned—and being the substratum of an infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable multitude of auspicious attributes;

and having established that He is the Self of all, since the entire aggregate of conscious and unconscious entities proceeds by His own volition, the scriptures teach that His worship, along with its constituent parts, is the means for attaining Him. (79)
As it has been said:

"This self consists entirely of nirvāṇa; it is composed of knowledge and is stainless. Phenomena characterized by suffering, ignorance, and impurity belong to primordial nature (prakṛti), not to the self."
Thus, because they are rooted in karma produced through the contact with primordial nature (*prakṛti*), these qualities are not prompted by the true nature of the Self; this is the meaning.
By distinguishing between what is attained and what is unattained, it is stated that these qualities belong to primordial nature alone. [As it is said:
"In a Brahmin endowed with knowledge and discipline, in a cow, in an elephant..."
"And the wise see the same in a dog as well as in an outcaste" (Gītā 5.18).

Those whose intellect discriminates the true nature of the Self—which is conjoined with the material nature (*prakṛti*) manifesting in the forms of gods, animals, humans, and immobile beings—are the "wise.

Being possessed of the knowledge of the reality of the Self as dissociated from each of those specific material natures, they perceive the Self as being of a uniform nature even while existing in various extremely dissimilar forms; thus they are called "those who see the same."
Regarding this, it is said:
"In this very world, rebirth is conquered by those whose minds are established in equanimity;
for Brahman is flawless and equal, therefore they are established in Brahman."

Thus, the meaning is as follows: "Flawless" means free from defects such as contact with the specific natures of gods and other beings; the entire reality of the Self, abiding in its own essential nature, is equal because it possesses the single form of knowledge whose nature is *nirvāṇa*.

It has already been stated that for such a Self, the fact that its sole essence is subservience to the Blessed One, its being governed by Him, and its having Him as its sole support is taught in the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇas through terms such as "His body" (*taccharīra*) and "His form" (*tan-tanu*), as well as through grammatical coordination (*samānādhikaraṇya*) with Him. (81)
For this divine illusion of mine, consisting of the gunas, is difficult to overcome;
but those who take refuge in Me alone cross over this illusion.

Thus, it is stated that liberation from this transmigratory existence— which consists of the soul's contact with *prakṛti* composed of various qualities produced by its own karma— is not possible without taking refuge in the Blessed Lord;
as also established by such scriptural passages as, "There is no other path for going," and "By Me,
whose form is unmanifest, all this world is pervaded."
All beings abide in me, yet I do not abide in them.
And yet the beings do not dwell in Me; behold My divine yoga.
Thus, by virtue of the possession of all powers, the diversity of His own sovereignty has been described. He says:
"Pervading this entire universe, I remain with but a single fraction.
Having entered as the Self—even with a ten-millionth part of Myself—this world of infinite, diverse, and most wonderful forms, I sustain it all through My volition.
The meaning is: "By means of this form, having pervaded [the universe], I stand as an ocean of immeasurable and noble qualities of infinite great majesty, a source of unsurpassed wonder.
This is what he says:
If there is unity, there is multiplicity; and if there is multiplicity, there is unity.
The nature of Brahman is inconceivable; how could one possibly know it?

Thus, though being one alone as the Ruler, He enters into the diverse sentient and insentient entities as their inner self; assuming various forms and causing them to perform their respective actions, He indeed assumes manifold appearances.

In this same way, though He remains as the Lord of all, possessing an infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable multitude of auspicious qualities, He enters and sustains this entire, wondrous, and multiform universe with but a small portion of Himself, yet abides in a state of multiplicity through His immanence within it.

The Supreme Person, Nārāyaṇa, who is the Supreme Brahman, the unsurpassed wonder, resembling a dark blue cloud, with eyes as large and pure as the petals of a lotus, possessing thousands of rays like the thousand-rayed sun— he alone abides in the supreme ether, established in the cave of the heart, as established by such Vedic scriptures as, "He who knows Him hidden in the secret cave, in the supreme ether," and "In that imperishable, in the supreme ether. (82)

For any entity whatsoever other than Brahman, it is impossible for that which possesses a single nature, a single causal capacity, and a single form, to be joined with another form, another nature, or another capacity. However, because this Supreme Brahman is of a different genus from all things, it possesses the nature of all things and is endowed with all capacities.

The meaning is that it is not contradictory for a single entity to possess both a manifold and infinite variety of forms and, furthermore, through its connection with an infinite and immeasurable wonder, to possess a single form; therefore, because they are identical in being mere entities (*vastumātra*), it is not reasonable to consider them a contradiction. As it has been said:
"The powers of all things are the domain of inconceivable knowledge."
Therefore, those powers of being, such as creation and the rest, belong to Brahman.
"O best of ascetics, it is just as heat belongs to fire.

By this it is meant: since a capacity is observed in even a single entity among all things such as fire and water, it is not reasonable to think that it does not exist in other entities of a different class; for even if it is not seen in water and the like, it exists in fire, which is of a different class from them.
Just as powers such as luminosity and heat are observed [in fire], it is not logical to infer total similarity in Brahman, which is of a different genus from all things;
therefore, the meaning is that Brahman alone possesses diverse and infinite powers. Thus he says:
This world is a great marvel, yet it is the form of that Great Soul; O Kṛṣṇa, I have been united with you, the most excellent of wonders.
Thus [it is said].
This has been ascertained through the labor of studying the various and infinite collections of Śruti texts and their authoritative commentaries.

For indeed, creation and dissolution—unperceived by other means of knowledge, possessing immeasurable transformations, and characterized by a sequence fixed within a single fundamental principle—[are established].
The various scriptural passages concerning Brahman declare it to be "blameless, stainless, consciousness, bliss, changeless,
partless, actionless, peaceful, devoid of qualities," and so forth; some scriptures further state that Brahman is devoid of qualities and has the nature of pure knowledge.
"There is no diversity whatsoever here; he goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were diversity.
"But where for him everything has become the Self alone, by what and whom should he see? By what and whom should he distinguish? There are several such scriptural passages that deny plurality.

He who is all-knowing and all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge, who, having fashioned all forms and assigned names, remains speaking—after him, as the Person, all moments of time were born from the lightening-flash. He is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true; thus [he exists] throughout the entire world.

Having negated all qualities understood as things to be abandoned, certain Śruti passages declare the infinity of unsurpassed auspicious qualities, the possession of omniscience and omnipotence, the manifestation of all names and forms, and the sustaining of everything— such as "All this is indeed Brahman, from which it is born, into which it dissolves, and in which it breathes" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1), "All this has that as its self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7), and "Being one, he manifests himself in many ways" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.90.2). Having thus established that the world created by Brahman possesses various forms, they teach its identity with Him.
And some teach [the following]:

"Having conceived of the self and the impeller as distinct; having conceived of the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the impeller—Prajāpati desired, 'May I create offspring. [He meditated upon] the Lord of the universe, the Self and Ruler, the auspicious, the infallible, Him who is the supreme among lords."

"Maheśvara, the supreme deity among deities, the controller of all, the lord of all"— such passages [establish] that Brahman is distinct from everything else, and that Brahman possesses sovereignty over all as the one to be ruled; likewise, they establish that the Lord (Īśvara) has everything as his subordinate and is the master of all.

"The Teacher has entered within; He is the Self of all people, this Self of yours, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. "Of whom the earth is the body," "of whom the waters are the body," "of whom fire is the body," and so forth, up to "of whom the unmanifest is the body," "of whom the imperishable is the body," "of whom death is the body," and "of whom the Self is the body"—[this passage teaches] the relationship of body and self between everything that is distinct from Brahman and Brahman itself.
"Some [scriptures] show [the opposite]," they say.
(84) One must describe how the non-contradiction of various types of statements and the non-abandonment of their primary meaning occur as is possible.
And it has been described that the scriptural texts concerning changelessness possess their primary meaning precisely by avoiding any transformation of essential nature.
And the discourses on the absence of qualities (*nirguṇavāda*) are established as being intent upon the negation of those qualities that are to be abandoned as belonging to *prakṛti*.

Furthermore, the discourses negating plurality are well-guarded in their sense that all things—sentient and insentient—are modes of the one Brahman by virtue of being its body; thus, Brahman alone exists in every mode as the self of everything.

Statements such as "being distinct in every way," "possessing lordship," "having the form of a multitude of all auspicious qualities," "having true desires," and "having true resolves" are well-protected precisely because of that [scriptural] acceptance.
Furthermore, the teaching that [Brahman] consists solely of knowledge and bliss refers to that which is other than everything else— the Lord of All, the substratum of all auspicious qualities,
the Sovereign of All, the Remainder of All, the Support of All, the cause of the origin, maintenance, and dissolution of all, the faultless, and the changeless.

Since it has been established that for the Supreme Brahman, who is the Self of all, the attribute that defines its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is precisely knowledge in the form of bliss that is opposed to impurity, and because its very nature is also knowledge due to its self-luminosity, [the doctrine of] non-duality is maintained.

Furthermore, the monistic doctrines are firmly established precisely by demonstrating that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is primary in the sense of the relationship between the body and the Self. (85)
This being the case, what meaning—whether non-difference, difference, or a dual nature—is established as that which is to be known through the Vedāntas?
Since everything is to be known through the Vedas, everything is thereby established.
Because Brahman alone exists in every manner as the body of all things, non-difference is established.

Brahman is indeed one, yet it exists in a state of manifoldness through its modes consisting of the diverse categories of sentient and insentient entities; thus, there is both difference and non-difference.

Difference is established because of the distinctness of the essential nature and characteristics of insentient matter, sentient beings, and the Lord, as well as their lack of confusion with one another.

(86) Now, an objection may be raised: from such texts as "That thou art, O Śvetaketu" and "For him, that alone is the delay," it is understood that the knowledge of oneness alone is the means for liberation, which is characterized as the supreme human goal.
This is not so;

for it is said, "Having perceived the Self and the Impeller as distinct, he, being favored by Him, thereafter attains immortality. Thus, having perceived the Self and the Impeller—the Inner Controller—as distinct, one is favored by that Supreme Self due to the cause of that knowledge of distinction, and thereby attains immortality.
It is understood that "it goes" refers precisely to the knowledge of the distinctness of the Self from its Controller as the direct means for attaining immortality.
(87) If it is argued that this must be accepted as referring to the attainment of the non-ultimate, qualified Brahman because it contradicts the scriptural texts on unity, we reply:
since it is heard that the knowledge of distinctness itself is the direct means for attaining immortality, why should the opposite not be the case?
This is what is meant:
when there is a conflict between two equal [authorities], their respective domains must be distinguished by means of non-contradiction.
If it is asked, "How is there non-contradiction? [the answer follows].

Because the individual self (*jīvātman*) is a mode (*prakāra*) of the Supreme Brahman—which exists as the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*)—by virtue of being its body, it is denoted by the word "Thou" (*tvam*), [the meaning being] that you are indeed that Brahman which is the mode of that [self].
It is precisely in this way that the meaning of that sentence is to be understood.

Since the Supreme Self, which exists as the very essence of such an individual self, is free from all defects and possesses the power of true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpatva*), [it is established as the ultimate reality].

The meaning of this statement— that the distinctness [of the Self] consists in its being a mine of infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable multitudes of auspicious qualities— is something that has already been stated repeatedly.

Regarding the passage, "Having understood the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the impeller," the inherent natures of the entity that constitutes the object of enjoyment are its insentience, its lack of ultimate reality, and its constant state of being subject to modification, and so forth.

The essential natures of the experiencer—the individual self (jīvātman), whose own nature is pure and unlimited knowledge and bliss—are as follows: the contraction and expansion of various forms of knowledge caused by beginningless ignorance in the form of karma, association with insentient objects that serve as the experienced world, and liberation through the meditation upon the Supreme Self. Furthermore, it should be understood that the Supreme Brahman exists in three modes: abiding as the inner ruler (antaryāmin) within both such an experiencer and the experienced object, and abiding in its own nature as the locus of an immeasurable multitude of attributes.
This is the meaning.

(88) Regarding the Sadvidyā, the venerable former teachers have explained that in the passage "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), the Brahman to be meditated upon is endowed with qualities (*saguṇa*), and the fruit is the attainment of that qualified Brahman.
As stated by the author of the *Vākya* [the Vākyakāra]: "It is appropriate because of meditation on Him as possessing those qualities."

And it has been explained by the teacher Dramiḍa, who speaks of the option regarding knowledge (*vidyā-vikalpa*): "Even if one does not mentally pursue the multitude of qualities of the deity as something distinct [from the Self], nevertheless, one worships the deity as possessing internal qualities; thus, even in that case, the deity is attained as one endowed with qualities."
Being focused on his own Self and established in the knowledge of the True (sadvijñāna),

he should not mentally pursue a multitude of qualities belonging to a deity that is distinct [from himself], even if— like one established in the Dahara-vidyā— he were not to recollect the multitude of auspicious qualities such as freedom from sin (apahatapāpmatva) as being separate from the Deity.
Nevertheless, one worships a deity who possesses internal qualities (*antarguṇa*), because the entire multitude of auspicious qualities is inseparable from the very nature of the deity.

Even when a deity is worshipped through some quality common to other supreme deities— such as being the cause of the entire universe— the deity is, in reality, worshipped as distinguished by the full collection of all auspicious qualities that are inherently connected to its essential nature.
Therefore, the meaning is that Brahman with attributes (*saguṇa*) alone is what is to be attained even there; thus, there is an option (*vikalpa*) between the Sadvidyā and the Daharavidyā.
(89) Now, it has been stated that the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is the inner ruler (*antaryāmī*) of every living being and that everything is governed by Him.
This being so, no one qualified for the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions would be observed.
Only one who is capable of engaging in action or desisting from it by his own intellect is fit for injunctions and prohibitions, such as "one should do this" or "one should not do that.
Yet such a person is not observed.
For it has been established that the Supreme Self is the impeller and the cause of all activity; He is the director of everyone, as He governs everything.
And thus it is heard in scripture: "It is he alone who causes that person to perform good deeds whom he wishes to lead up from these worlds;
it is he alone who causes that person to perform evil deeds whom he wishes to lead down.
Because he causes both good and evil deeds to be performed, there would also be the charge of cruelty. (90)

To this it is replied: having generally provided for all sentient beings the connection with the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), the connection with the power of activity (*pravṛttiśakti*), and so forth— comprising the entire apparatus of engagement and withdrawal— the Supreme Self, who exists as the sovereign (*śeṣī*) by entering within and exercising control as the permissive supervisor (*anumantṛ*) while serving as their support, performs the engagement, withdrawal, and so on himself, being one whose powers are deposited in them.

The Supreme Self remains indifferent while observing one who acts in this manner; therefore, everything is logically consistent. Furthermore, the status of being the instigator of good and evil deeds pertains to specific, established objects and is not common to all.

But as for one who has himself excessively engaged in what is entirely favorable, the Blessed One, being pleased with him, bestows the gift of the application of a virtuous intellect and personally impels him toward what is auspicious.
On the other hand, to one who has excessively engaged in what is unfavorable, the Blessed One, imparting a cruel intellect, himself impels him toward cruel actions alone.
As it was said by the Blessed One:
To those who are constantly devoted and worship Me with love,
I give that yoga of discernment by which they come to Me.
Out of compassion for them alone, I, dwelling within their very self, destroy the darkness born of ignorance with the radiant lamp of knowledge.
"Those hateful and cruel ones, the lowest of men in the worlds of transmigration, those inauspicious ones, I cast perpetually into demonic wombs alone. (91) Thus [it is said].
This very Supreme Person, who has become the Supreme Brahman, [is the one] for whom the entire heap of sins accumulated over many births has been exhausted by an unsurpassed accumulation of merit.

[He is] one who has attained the state of being turned toward [the Lord] through taking refuge at the lotus-feet of the Supreme Person; who possesses the realization of the true nature of reality as understood from the scriptures, augmented by the instructions of a true teacher; who is endowed with self-qualities such as tranquility, self-control, austerity, purity, forbearance, uprightness, discrimination between what is fearful and what is fearless, compassion, non-violence, and so forth, which increase day by day; and who is devoted to the performance of obligatory and occasional rites appropriate to his caste and stage of life for the worship of the Supreme Person, while abandoning prohibited actions.

It is attainable solely through that devotion consisting of uninterrupted, supreme, and most intense meditation—which has become direct perception—whose sole purpose is [the Lord], and which is obtained by one who has surrendered self and possessions at the pair of lotus-feet of the Supreme Person; who is pleased by constant praise, remembrance, salutation, worship, prostration, circumambulation, glorification, hearing of His qualities, speaking of them, meditation, adoration, and obeisance performed out of devotion; and whose darkness of heart has been destroyed by the grace of the Supreme Person, the Most Compassionate One, who is moved by such devotion.
This has been stated by the supreme preceptors, the venerable Yāmunācāryapāda: "It is attainable through the yoga of exclusive and ultimate devotion by one whose mind is cultivated in both ways.
This means: by one whose internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) has been refined by the yoga of knowledge and the yoga of action.
And so says the Śruti:
He who knows both knowledge and ignorance together—
having crossed over death by means of ignorance, he enjoys immortality through knowledge.

Thus [it is said]. Here, by the word "ignorance" (avidyā), the previously mentioned ritual action (karman)—such as the conduct of the social classes and stages of life—is denoted because it is other than knowledge (vidyā); and by the word "knowledge" (vidyā), meditation in the form of devotion is denoted. As it has been stated: "Relying on knowledge, he performed very many sacrifices; having established himself in the knowledge of Brahman, he crossed over death by means of ignorance."
Thus it is said: "One who knows Him thus becomes immortal here; there is no other path for the journey.
Those who know Him become immortal.
The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme."
Thus, [in passages such as] "He who knows that supreme Brahman, he knows Brahman; he becomes Brahman itself," and so forth,
the word "knowing" (*vedana*) denotes meditation (*dhyāna*) alone,
because it has the same meaning as [the injunction] "it is to be meditated upon intensely" (*nididhyāsitavya*), and so on.
He further qualifies that very meditation: "This Self is not to be attained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing;
only by whomsoever this [Self] chooses, by him is He attained; to him this Self reveals His own form.
It is attained only through meditation that has taken the form of devotion, and not merely by itself.
"One does not attain [the goal] by mere knowledge," because solitary [knowledge] is prohibited.

What is meant is this: when this seeker of liberation—who is devoted to meditation and the like in the form of knowledge prescribed in the Vedāntas—experiences an unsurpassed and infinite joy in that very meditation, at that very moment he attains the Supreme Person.
As it was said by the Blessed One:
"That Supreme Person, O Pārtha, is attainable by unswerving devotion;
for in this way, O Arjuna, I am reachable only through unswerving devotion."
To know it, to see it in its true essence, and to enter into it, O scorcher of the foe.
Through devotion, one comes to know Me in truth—both who I am and what I am;
then, having known Me in truth, one enters into Me immediately thereafter.
Thus [it is said]. The meaning is that immediately thereafter, one enters [the Supreme] out of devotion (*bhakti*).
Furthermore, devotion is indeed a specific kind of knowledge (*jñāna-viśeṣa*) which is supremely dear, has no other purpose, and brings about an indifference toward everything else.
Therefore, it is logical that one becomes worthy of being chosen by that Supreme Self; thus, the meaning of the Śruti is that "He is attained by Him."

The producer of such a specific knowledge consisting of supreme devotion is precisely the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*) supported by action preceded by the aforementioned knowledge that is accumulated day by day.
As it was stated by the venerable Parāśara: "By a person who possesses the conduct appropriate for their caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*), the Supreme Person..."
Viṣṇu is the path to be propitiated; there is no other that brings him satisfaction.

Thus it is said: The Supreme Person, who is the Supreme Brahman, descended to the surface of the earth for the sake of uplifting the entire world; he himself has declared this—listen to how one devoted to his own duty attains perfection.
Since from Him proceeds the activity of all beings and by Him all this is pervaded,
a human being attains perfection by worshipping Him through his own duty.
Thus, it is attainable solely through devotion transformed according to the sequence described above.

This [truth] has been demonstrated by a multitude of scriptural passages whose meanings are made perfectly clear by the ancient commentaries on the Vedas and Vedāntas, which are accepted by unimpeachable authorities such as Bodhāyana, Ṭaṅka, Dramiḍa, Guhadeva, Kapardin, Bhāruciprabhṛti, and others.

By this, those who follow the doctrines of the Cārvākas, Śākyas, Aulūkyas, Ākṣapādas, Kṣapaṇakas, Kapilas, and Patañjali—being outside the Veda—are refuted along with those of false views who falsely rely upon the Vedas.
Even for those who rely on the Vedas, there is a perversion of things as they truly exist; such people are said by Manu himself to be equal to outsiders:
"Whatever Smṛtis are outside the Veda, and whatever false views there may be—all these are fruitless after death, for they are declared to be grounded in darkness."

Thus [it is said]: for those whose innate quality (*guṇa*) is precisely the supreme *sattva* untouched by *rajas* and *tamas*, there alone is a taste for the Veda and an understanding of the true nature of the Vedic meaning.
As it is stated in the *Mātsya-purāṇa*: "There are those who are mixed, as well as those characterized by *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. (94)

Thus, having described the classification of the kalpas— some being mixed (*saṃkīrṇa*), some abounding in *sattva*, some abounding in *rajas*, and some abounding in *tamas*— it is further stated that the description of the majesty of the principles (*tattva*) consisting of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* is performed by Brahmā, who is composed of those very qualities (*guṇa*), within the Purāṇas proclaimed in each respective kalpa.
In whichever Purāṇa was proclaimed by Brahmā in the past during a particular Kalpa, the greatness of that very Purāṇa is described according to its own essential nature.
Thus it is said: "In particular,
it is declared that the majesty of Agni-Śiva is proclaimed in the Tāmasa [scriptures],
while the wise know that the majesty of Brahmā is predominant in the Rājasa [scriptures]."
In the Sāttvika kalpas, the majesty of Hari is supreme;
in those very kalpas, those perfected in yoga shall attain the highest goal.
In the confluences of the Sarasvatī...

And so forth. This is what is meant: because Brahman is the primordial knower (*ādikṣetrajña*), even in him there is an increase of *sattva* on certain days, of *rajas* on others, and of *tamas* on still others.
As it was said by the Blessed One:
"There is nothing on earth, nor in heaven among the gods, again..."
That which is the *sattva* (pure being) liberated from these three qualities born of *prakṛti*.
Thus [it is said], for according to the Śruti: "He who first created Brahmā and who indeed bestowed the Vedas upon him.
Since even Brahmā is a created being and is subject to the authority of the scriptures, he is understood to be a *kṣetrajña* (knower of the field).

Regarding those ancient texts (*purāṇas*) proclaimed by Brahmā during days predominantly characterized by *sattva*, as well as others [predominantly characterized by *rajas* and *tamas*], in the event of mutual contradictions among them—

It is understood that this was spoken by Brahmā, who is established in *sattva*, for the very purpose of determining the Purāṇas— that those which are declared to be *sāttvika* are indeed authentic (*yathārtha*), while others that contradict them are inauthentic (*ayathārtha*). Furthermore, the effects of *sattva* and the other qualities have been described by the Blessed Lord himself.
From *sattva* arises knowledge, and from *rajas*, greed;
from *tamas* arise negligence and delusion, as well as ignorance itself.

O Pārtha, that intellect which understands both engagement and withdrawal, what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, fear and fearlessness, as well as bondage and liberation— that intellect is of the nature of sattva.
O Pārtha, that intellect which perceives dharma and adharma, as well as what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, incorrectly, is of the nature of passion (rājasa).
That intellect which, enveloped by darkness, perceives unrighteousness as righteousness and regards all objects in a perverted manner— that, O Pārtha, is tāmasī.
Thus, having indeed acquired all the contents of the Purāṇas from the presence of Brahmā, the authors of the Purāṇas composed them all. As it has been said:
"I shall relate [it] just as it was formerly told by Dakṣa and the other most excellent sages."
Being thus questioned, the Blessed One, the Grandfather born from the lotus, replied.
Thus [it is said].
If it is asked, "How can there be no contradiction among the Vedic statements, which are not of human origin and are mutually contradictory?"—
the absence of contradiction has already been stated previously through the determination of their intended meaning (*tātparya*).

Moreover, even though it may appear thus contradictory— that one should meditate upon and intensely contemplate this entire universe after establishing the vital breath (prāṇa) together with its causes within the mind, and [finally] within the Supreme Self at the end of sound (nādānta)—
[the truth is that] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are all produced from Him;
He is not a cause [of being produced].
But the cause is to be meditated upon:

Śambhu, endowed with all sovereignty and the Lord of all, is to be meditated upon in the midst of space—he than whom there is nothing higher or lower, than whom there is none smaller or greater; he stands alone, firm like a tree in heaven.
Therefore, all this is filled by the Puruṣa; that which is higher than that is formless and free from suffering. Those who know this become immortal, while others enter only into suffering.
He has faces, heads, and necks everywhere; he dwells in the secret cave of the heart of all beings.
And the Blessed One is all-pervading; therefore, Śiva is omnipresent.
When there was darkness, then there was neither day nor night, neither being nor non-being; Śiva alone was the absolute.
That is the Imperishable, that is the most excellent splendor of Savitṛ; from it, ancient wisdom issued forth.
Such statements as these, along with the fact that Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman, have already been established previously;
therefore, how can there be no contradiction between them?
This [objection] is far too simplistic.
The Vedas, along with their auxiliary limbs, augmented by the logic of the words proclaimed by the most eminent among the knowers of the Veda,
declare that Hari is the cause of the birth and other states of the universe.
"From which the origin, etc., of this [world proceed"; or "from which indeed these beings are born, by which, once born, they live, and into which they enter at the time of their passing."
"One should desire to understand that; that is Brahman"—thus it is understood that Brahman is the cause of the origin and so forth of the world.
And that [Brahman] is to be understood from the sections concerning the creation and dissolution of the world.

In the passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second," the Supreme Cause is established by the word "Being" (sat) through its aspects as the material cause, the efficient cause, and the inner ruler of the world.
It is understood that this very meaning is expressed by the word "Brahman" in another Vedic recension (śākhā) in the passage, "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman alone. Thus,
it is understood that Brahman is denoted by this word "Sat" (Being).

This very same meaning is understood from another recensional branch (*śākhāntara*): "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone; there was nothing else whatsoever that blinked. Here, it is understood that the Self itself is denoted by the terms *sat* and *brahman*.

Likewise, in another recensional branch: "Verily, Nārāyaṇa alone existed; there was no Brahmā, no Īśāna, nor these two, heaven and earth, nor the stars. It is thus determined that Nārāyaṇa alone is designated by such terms as *sat*, *brahman*, *ātman*, and others which denote the supreme cause. (97)
"That which the seers weave within the ocean," and so forth; "No one has grasped him from above, nor from across, nor from the middle; no one rules over him; his name is Great Glory."
"His form does not stand within the range of vision; no one sees him with the eye.
He is fashioned by the heart, by insight, and by the mind. Those who know him thus become immortal.

Having thus established his transcendence over everything, and having prohibited [the existence of] anything beyond him by stating, "No one rules over him; there is nothing whatsoever higher than he," [the text proceeds].
The phrase "born from the waters, Hiraṇyagarbha" [and so on] consists of eight verses; this indicates syntactic unity with that [passage].
Furthermore, that section concerning the Great Person (Mahāpuruṣa), including the statement "Hrī and Lakṣmī are your two wives," illuminates that [the subject] is indeed Nārāyaṇa.
This meaning is elaborated in the Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka.

Beginning with "The thousand-headed God," and continuing with "He is Brahman, He is Śiva, He is Indra, He is the Imperishable, the Supreme, the Self-ruling," [the text] employs in all the Vedic branches every term— such as Akṣara, Śiva, Śambhu, Parabrahman, Parajyotis, Paratattva, Parāyaṇa, Paramātman, and so forth— which is intended to establish the Supreme Reality.
By virtue of their respective qualities, these terms are applied exclusively to Nārāyaṇa, establishing that everything else apart from Him is His substratum and subject to His control.

Having established that [the individual soul] is a part of Him and has Him as its essence, it is further demonstrated that even Brahmā and Śiva possess His nature as manifestations (*vibhūti*), since they share the same form as Indra and the other deities.
Furthermore, this passage is solely intent upon establishing the supreme reality alone; nothing else whatsoever is enjoined here.

In other passages, such as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," the practice of meditation and so forth is enjoined for that Brahman who, as established in this passage, exists as superior to all.

Therefore, the passage beginning with "Then one should merge the vital breath into the mind along with the organs" and so forth, instructs the meditation on Nārāyaṇa alone, who is the Supreme Brahman; for it teaches that after withdrawing the entire collection of modifications—the organs, the vital breath, and so forth—into the Supreme Self, the cause of all, one should meditate upon that very Supreme Self as the Lord of all.
This is because His sovereignty over everything is established by the words "the Lord of the universe" and "there is no one who rules over Him."

Therefore, because Śambhu—who is endowed with all sovereignty and is the Lord of All—is to be meditated upon in the midst of space, the meditation on Nārāyaṇa alone, who is the supreme cause and is denoted by the word "Śambhu," is prescribed. This is because the passage beginning with "And who is to be meditated upon? and ending with "But the Cause is to be meditated upon" aims solely at the fact that while the effect is not to be meditated upon, the Cause alone is to be meditated upon. Furthermore, his status as the supreme cause and his being denoted by the word "Śambhu" are established in the section whose sole purpose is to demonstrate the supreme cause.

Since the Nārāyaṇānuvāka itself establishes [Nārāyaṇa as the object], it is not appropriate for an injunction regarding the object of meditation to posit a different meaning that contradicts it by suggesting that the Cause alone is to be meditated upon.
(101) Furthermore, as for the claim that in the passage "that which is higher than that," something other than Puruṣa is perceived to be superior; [this is incorrect].

Moreover, because there is nothing higher than that, nothing smaller or greater than that, and because there is nothing else whatsoever higher than that— meaning that in no way is there anything other than the Puruṣa that possesses the status of being "higher"— the term *aṇīyas* refers to subtlety (*sūkṣmatva*).
"Greater" (*jyāyastva*) means being the Lord of all.

Because He is all-pervading and the Lord of all, there is no one else distinct from Him who possesses either minuteness (*aṇīyastva*) or greatness (*jyāyastva*). Since it is stated, "There is nothing smaller and nothing greater," the greatness of anything other than the Puruṣa is negated; therefore, it has been refuted that the status of being supreme (*paratva*) belongs to anyone else.
What, then, is the meaning of this statement?

At the beginning of this section, having asserted that knowledge of the Person is the cause of immortality and that there is no other path for proceeding—stating, "Only by knowing Him does one go beyond death; there is no other path for going"—[the text proceeds] from that which is higher than...
By the concluding statement, "There is nothing else beyond this; by that Person all this is filled," the state of being superior to everything has been established.

Since the reality of the Person (*puruṣatattva*) alone is the highest, therefore that reality of the Person which is the highest is itself formless and free from affliction. Those who know this become immortal, whereas others surely enter into suffering; thus, the fact that knowledge of the Person is the cause of immortality and that anything other than it is a wrong path has been asserted and concluded with its supporting reason.
Otherwise, this would contradict both the introductory context and the formal proposition.
It is already known from such passages as "the eternal, auspicious, and infallible" that the word *śiva* intends the Puruṣa alone, by virtue of his association with the quality of purity (*śuddhi*).
Immediately thereafter, [the text] states that the Puruṣa alone is denoted by the word *śiva*: "The Puruṣa is indeed the Great Lord; he is the impeller of *sattva*."

By the very same reasoning, everything beginning with "He is neither existent nor non-existent, he is Śiva alone" is to be understood. Furthermore, regarding that Person whose possibility of equals or superiors has been eliminated by the statement "no one rules over him," his status as Maheśvara is established in this section— "smaller than the smallest"— by virtue of being denoted by the vowel *ā*, which is the source of the *praṇava* (the seed-syllable of the Vedas), through his being the inner essence of the Vedas and so forth.
Having established this, it has been stated that [the Self] is to be meditated upon as residing within the space situated in the middle of the small lotus.
This is the meaning: the *praṇava* is said to be the source (*prakṛti*) of the entire Veda, and the letter *a* (*akāra*) is the source of the *praṇava*.

The Veda, which is a modification of the *praṇava*, is dissolved into the *praṇava*, its own material cause (*prakṛti*). The *praṇava* also, being a modification of the letter *a* (*akāra*), is dissolved into the letter *a*, its own material cause. That which is the supreme denotable object (*vācya*) of that letter *a*—which is the material cause of the *praṇava*—is indeed Maheśvara. Thus, he who is denoted by the letter *a*, the material cause of the entire class of denoters, is Nārāyaṇa, the material cause of the entire class of denotables.
This means he who is Maheśvara.
As it was said by the Blessed One:
"I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire world."
There is nothing whatsoever else higher than Me, O Dhanañjaya.
Among letters, I am the letter *a*.

Thus, from the Śruti: "A is Brahman," and "The letter 'a' is indeed all speech. It is perfectly clear that the entire class of signifiers has the letter 'a' as its primordial source (prakṛti), and the entire class of signifieds has Brahman as its primordial source.
Therefore, since it has been established that Brahman is denoted by the syllable *akāra*, it is proven that Nārāyaṇa alone is Maheśvara as denoted by *akāra*.

His status as being superior to all else is elaborated in the *Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka*, which is devoted to establishing the specific nature of the absolute reality (*paratattva*) through the verse beginning, "The thousand-headed God...

This very supreme reality, established by this [text] which is not subordinate to anything else, is [also] expressed by some word or other in all those other statements that are subordinate to something else.

Having understood that "it is indeed that which is being perceived," the author of the Sūtras has determined—on the basis of the perspective of the scriptures—that the instruction is like that given to Vāmadeva.
Thus, since this Supreme Brahman is understood in some places through words such as "Brahman" or "Śiva," there is no possibility of [the status of] supremacy belonging solely to Brahman or Śiva;
for in this section, which is not intended for anything else, those two are established as being manifestations (vibhūti) of Him, equal to Indra and the other deities.

In some places, the Supreme Brahman is denoted by such terms as "ether" (*ākāśa*) and "vital breath" (*prāṇa*); thus, the elemental ether and the vital breath do not possess supremacy. Furthermore, as for this doubt that was raised: "Now, in this city of Brahman, there is a small lotus-palace; within it is the small inner ether; that which is inside that is what one must seek, and that is what one must desire to understand."

Thus, in this passage, having established the material cause of the universe by means of the word "ether" (*ākāśa*), it is taught that a certain specific reality existing within it is to be sought after. Since this ether is heard to be the bearer of name and form (*nāmarūpa*), and since in the *Puruṣasūkta* the Puruṣa is seen to be the agent of name and form,
it is understood— by those who have not studied the Vedas— that there is something other than the Puruṣa (who is a synonym for ether) that is to be sought after and worshipped.
This objection is raised by those who have not seen the scriptures;
for therein, the Śruti itself provides the answer:
"And the author of the Vākya [Bhāṣya] says: 'In this small space within, what is there that should be sought after, that should be understood?'"

When it is enjoined that "or rather, He is to be sought after," [the text] establishes the infinite greatness and the status as the substratum of the entire universe of this Supreme Person— who is denoted by the word "ether" (ākāśa)— through the passage beginning, "As large as this external ether is, so large is this ether within the heart. Then, by the phrase "desires are contained within Him," the eightfold set of qualities beginning with freedom from sin and ending with true resolve is indicated by the word "desires" (kāma).

By the very words of the Śruti, "That which is within it is to be sought," it has been resolved that—just as with the Supreme Person—the eightfold qualities of the Supreme Person are also intended to be known through the earth; thus, all [objections] are answered.
This is what is meant: [the answer to] the objection, "What is there in this that is to be sought? is that everything [is contained] within it.

The resolution is that the qualities of being the creator of the world, its support, its controller, its sovereign, as well as freedom from sin and other such attributes, do indeed exist. And thus says the author of the Vākya: "In Him, that which is within is the designation of desires. Desires (kāmāḥ) are so called because they are desired (kāmyante).
The meaning is that these are qualities such as being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*).

This is what is being said: within that Supreme Brahman—which is denoted by the term "the small ether" (*daharākāśa*) and whose play consists in the arising, expansion, and dissolution of the entire universe—there is contained the eightfold group of qualities, such as being free from evil, which are characterized by an absence of any limit or degree of excellence.
"Both of these are to be sought after and desired to be known.

As it is said: "Now, those who depart from here having discovered the Self and these true desires, for them there is freedom of movement in all worlds. Furthermore, regarding the statement whose intent is to establish that the Cause alone is the object of meditation, [it refers to] Viṣṇu, who is established as the Supreme Reality by statements not devoted to anything else.

His inclusion in the midst of [the categories of] effects should be understood as a voluntary descent by his own will for the benefit of the world, while he fulfills the enumeration of the principles (tattvas) that constitute his own nature.
Just as, through his divine play, the Supreme Being himself assumes the form of Upendra to complete the number of deities.
Just as there was the voluntary descent of the Supreme Brahman himself in the form of Daśaratha’s son to complete the enumeration of kings born of the Solar dynasty (*sūryavaṃśa*),
and just as there was the voluntary descent of the Blessed Lord into the house of Vasudeva to remove the burden of the earth while completing the enumeration of the Lunar dynasty (*somavaṃśa*);
it has already been stated previously that in the sections concerning creation and dissolution, Nārāyaṇa alone is established as the ultimate cause.

Furthermore, as for the fact that Rudra’s own universal sovereignty (*sarvaiśvarya*) was elaborated upon in the *Atharvaśiras*, that was stated because of the entry of the Supreme Self (Paramātman), according to the explicit statement of the Śruti itself: "He entered from within into the interior.
The meaning of this is established by the author of the Sūtras himself in the aphorism: "But the instruction is [given] through the vision of the scripture, as in the case of Vāmadeva.
As it has also been said by Prahlāda:
Because that which is immediate is all-pervading, I alone remain as that;
from me everything comes, I am everything, and everything exists within me, the eternal.
And so forth. Here, the reason "because [He] is all-pervading and infinite" is stated.

It has been explained that since the Supreme Self is all-pervading as the Self of everything—both conscious and unconscious—which constitutes His own body, all words denote the Supreme Self alone, who has the entire universe as His body.
Therefore, the word "I" denotes the Supreme Self Himself, who is the possessor (prakārin) of which my own self is a mode (prakāra).
Therefore, this is said:

"But one should grasp [the Self] as 'I' alone, because everything is produced from that," and so forth. By this, the author of the *Vākya* teaches the meditation on the grasping of the "I" (ahaṃgrahaṇopāsana), [stating] that the Supreme Self alone—possessing the gross and subtle sentient and insentient entities as its body—is both in the state of cause and in the state of effect, and thus everything [is He].
It has been stated, "Because that [self] is established," and by the author of the Sūtras as well: "But they acknowledge it as the Self and cause others to grasp it.
And in the Mahābhārata, in the dialogue between Brahmā and Rudra, Brahmā said to Rudra:
"Your inner self, mine, and those of others who are designated as embodied beings"—
thus, the Supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa exists as the inner self of Rudra, Brahmā, and all other embodied beings.
Likewise, in that very same [text]:
Viṣṇu is the self of the blessed Bhava of immeasurable splendor;
therefore, that Maheśvara endured the touch of the bowstring.
Thus it is said: "In that very place, these two foremost of the wise are remembered as being born from grace and wrath;
following the paths shown by Him, they are the agents of creation and dissolution."
Thus, the meaning is that Brahmā and Rudra, who follow the path shown by Nārāyaṇa abiding as the inner self (*antarātman*), are the agents of the tasks of creation and dissolution.

Those who assert a distinction between the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the material cause (*upādāna*) would indeed be outside the Veda, because they contradict the sūtras composed by those who know the Veda, such as: "From whom [proceeds] the birth, etc., of this [world]; and [He is] the material cause, so that there may be no contradiction with the [scriptural] promise and the illustrative examples," and so forth. (109)

In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second. It thought: "May I be many; may I procreate. That was the forest of Brahman, that was the tree from which they fashioned heaven and earth. Brahman stood over the worlds, upholding them.
All moments of time were born from the Person who is lightning. No one rules over him; his name is Great Gloriousness.

Furthermore, this contradicts all the Śruti texts, such as: "There is no diversity whatsoever here; the Puruṣa alone is the controller of all, the lord of all, this entire universe—whatever has been and whatever is to be—and he is the lord of immortality; there exists no other path for proceeding. Moreover, in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, within the sections concerning creation, maintenance, and dissolution, it is understood that this alone is the supreme reality.
As it is said in the Mahābhārata: "From what was all this world, both stationary and moving, created?
And unto whom does it go at the time of dissolution? Tell me that, O Grandfather."
Thus questioned,
Nārāyaṇa— the eternal, infinite self whose form is the universe—
spoke these and other words.
The sages, the ancestors, the gods, the great elements, and the constituent minerals—
this entire world, both moving and unmoving, has its origin in Nārāyaṇa.

And thus, this very Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa— beginning with "From which [proceeds] the birth, etc., of this"— is accepted without dispute by all the learned of the East, North, South, and West as being sufficient for the systematic determination of all dharmas and all principles; from it, Brahman is understood to be the cause of the world's birth and so forth.

It is universally accepted that [this text] proceeds with the sole purpose of establishing the specific nature of Brahman—beginning with the question, "What is the cause of that birth and so forth? and continuing with the passage "born from Viṣṇu," and so on—and likewise, in that very same work, it states:
"That which is called Prakṛti, whose nature consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest..."
And both of these, Puruṣa and Prakṛti, dissolve into the Supreme Self.
And the Supreme Self, the support of all, the Supreme Lord,
is celebrated in the Vedas and the Vedāntas by the name Viṣṇu.
Thus [it is said]. The meaning is that in all the Vedas and Vedāntas, this very one is celebrated by all words as the supreme cause.
Just as the Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka in all the Śrutis is engaged solely for the purpose of establishing the specific nature of the absolute Supreme Brahman, so too is this Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa.
"O knower of dharma, I desire to hear from you how this world [came to be]," [so says the text].
And it happened again, O highly fortunate one, as it will happen once more.
And from what, O Brahman, was this world composed, and from what did this world of moving and unmoving beings arise;
wherein it was dissolved, and wherein it will go to its dissolution?
Thus, having introduced the supreme Brahman with the words "What is it?", [it is stated that] the world has arisen from Viṣṇu and remains in Him alone;
He is the author of the maintenance and withdrawal of this world, and the world is He.
The Supreme among the supreme, the Highest Self established within the self,
devoid of specific designations such as form, color, and other such qualifiers.
That which is devoid of diminution, destruction, transformation, increase,
and birth can be described as merely "it exists."
Since he dwells everywhere and everything dwells within him,
for that reason he is recited by the learned as Vāsudeva.
That Brahman is supreme, eternal, unborn, undecaying, and immutable;
it is always of a single nature and stainless because of the absence of anything to be discarded.
All this is indeed that very same [reality], possessing the nature of both the manifest and the unmanifest;
likewise, it exists in the form of the Puruṣa and in the form of Time.
O Sage, he has transcended the primordial nature of all beings, their transformations, and the defects such as the qualities (guṇas);
having passed beyond all veils, he is the soul of all, by whom that which exists within the intermediate spaces of the worlds is pervaded.
He is the embodiment of all auspicious qualities; by a mere fragment of his own power, he has uplifted the multitude of living beings.
Having assumed vast bodies at will according to his desire, he has accomplished the welfare of the entire world.
He is the singular mass of qualities such as splendor, strength, sovereignty, great awakening, excellent heroism, and power;
he is the supreme among the supreme, the Lord of the high and the low, in whom no afflictions or other defects exist.
He is the Lord, consisting of both the individual and the collective, whose nature is unmanifest and whose nature is manifest;
the Lord of all, the seer of all, the knower of all, possessing all powers, known as the Supreme Lord.

That by which something is perceived—whether it be seen or realized—as being free from defects, pure, supreme, stainless, and of a single nature, is knowledge; that which is other than this is said to be ignorance.
Thus, [this work] is undertaken solely for the purpose of determining the specific nature of the Supreme Brahman.
All other Purāṇas are to be interpreted in a manner that does not contradict this;
furthermore, their focus on other subjects is understood from the manner in which they begin.
The portion that is entirely contradictory [to the truth] is to be disregarded because of its nature as darkness (*tamas*).
(112) But surely, even in this [system], there is the triad consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, who perform the acts of creation, preservation, and dissolution;
That Blessed One, the sole Janārdana, assumes that designation.
Thus, an equality among the three forms would appear;
but this is not so.
By the statement "Janārdana alone [is everything]," the identity of Janārdana himself with the entire phenomenal world, beginning with Brahmā and Śiva, is enjoined.
And he is the world—thus he explains what was previously stated: "He creates himself as the Creator (Sraṣṭṛ) and protects that which is to be protected as Viṣṇu;
and at the end, he is withdrawn as the Destroyer (Saṃhartṛ), being the self-sufficient Lord."
Thus, having simultaneously pointed out Brahmā as the creator and the created, and the destroyer and the destroyed,

by teaching the identity of everything with Viṣṇu, a distinction is seen in that the entities which are the created and the destroyed are merely manifestations (vibhūti) of Janārdana, who is the creator and the destroyer.
Since the words *janārdana* and *viṣṇu* are synonyms, [the text] refers to the manifestation (*vibhūti*) consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
For this very reason, it is stated that [Viṣṇu] is included within the manifestations by his own will for the sake of divine play (*līlā*).
This is as is stated immediately hereafter.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space,
as well as all the sense organs and the internal organ— that world which is indeed designated as the Puruṣa.
Since that very immutable one is the self of all beings and possesses universal form,
therefore the creation and so forth, which reside within beings, are for his benefit alone.
"He alone is the object of creation, and he is the creator of all; he alone protects and devours, and he is protected as well.

Viṣṇu, whose form is the entirety [of existence] through states such as Brahmā and others, is the most excellent, the giver of boons, and the one worthy of choice. (113) Here, the identity with the phenomenal world—which is mixed with that which is to be abandoned—is predicated in grammatical apposition [with Viṣṇu], even though [Viṣṇu] is faultless and changeless.

Anticipating the objection as to how [this] can be possible for Brahman, who consists of all auspicious qualities, he himself establishes it by stating, "since He alone is the imperishable one whose form is the universe and who is the Self of all beings.

Having made the proposition that Viṣṇu alone—who is the Lord of all and has become the Supreme Brahman—is the entire world, the reason is stated: "since He alone is the imperishable one whose form is the universe and who is the Self of all beings."
The meaning is that this Self of all beings has the universe as its body, because it is imperishable; and he will say later, "All that exists is indeed the body of Hari.
This is what is being stated.

Even for this imperishable Supreme Brahman Viṣṇu, identity with the universe—by virtue of having the universe as His body—is contradictory; thus, the respective natures of the Self and the body remain strictly distinct.

For Viṣṇu, the Lord of all who is of such a nature, there is an incarnation by His own will among the gods, animals, and humans included within the category of those to be governed within the phenomenal world, in order to be resorted to by each of them.

This [incarnation] occurs because Brahmā and the others, being subject to karma through their connection with the three types of mental dispositions (*bhāvanā*), are under the power of karma, whereas the Blessed One is the Supreme Brahman.

Furthermore, it is clearly stated in the sixth chapter, the *Śubhāśraya-prakaraṇa*, that Vāsudeva takes incarnation among the gods and others by his own will and in his own form for the benefit of the entire world.

Even in these incarnations in the forms of gods and so forth, his body is not composed of material elements; as stated in the *Mahābhārata*: "The body of this Supreme Self is not a structure formed from an aggregate of elements."
Thus it has been established.
And by the Śrutis: "Though being unborn, he is born in many ways; the wise perceive his source.

For those subject to karma, such as Brahmā and others, birth—which consists of entering bodies such as those of gods, characterized by specific configurations of elemental aggregates resulting from the transformation of *prakṛti* according to their respective karmas—is unavoidable even if they do not desire it.

But this Lord, the Sovereign of all, whose resolve is true, being of such a nature, though not performing good or evil births by his own will, is born in many ways among the gods and others for the benefit of the world, in his own unsurpassed and auspicious form. The meaning is that the wise—those who stand at the forefront of those possessing both steady and unsteady intellects—know the various births, that is, the manifold origins, of this very one, even though he does not perform good or evil births, owing to the infinity of his own auspicious qualities. (114)

Having raised the objection that there might be something superior to the Supreme Person, the Supreme Brahman—who has been established by such sūtras as "From which [proceeds] the origin and so forth of this [world]" and "And the material cause, because of the non-contradiction of the initial proposition and the illustrative examples"—as being other than Him who is the efficient and material cause of the entire universe;

[the author replies]: "But on account of commonality, it is for the sake of the intellect, like the feet. (Sūtra 3.2.33) "On account of commonality" means: because of the commonality of attributes such as being the cause of the world and possessing omniscience and omnipotence. The phrase "for the sake of the intellect" means: it is for the purpose of facilitating the understanding of the Supreme Self. "Like the feet" means: just as in the passage, "The earth is one foot of Him," the term "foot" is used figuratively for a part of the whole. Thus, the designation of a bridge, measure, connection, and distinction mentioned in the opponent's view are merely figurative. Therefore, there is nothing superior to the Supreme Brahman.

The author of the Sūtras himself refutes [the notion of spatial limitation] by stating: "Because it is logical due to the distinction of location, like light and so forth; and because other [limitations] are denied; and because of this [scripture], it is all-pervading, as indicated by the word 'Āyatana' and others" (Sūtra 2.3.29–30). Furthermore, this is stated in the Mānava Śāstra.
The dispeller of darkness appeared, desiring to create various beings;
he first created the waters alone, and into them he cast his seed.
Since it is heard that "Brahmā himself was born from him," his status as a *kṣetrajña* (knower of the field) is understood;
and thus there is a distinction between the Supreme Person who is the creator and Brahmā who is created by Him.
This [being] was previously remembered by him as Nārāyaṇa;
emitted by him, that Puruṣa is celebrated in the world as Brahmā.
This is also because of the specific mention of his name.

Likewise, in the *Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa*, it is established that Hiraṇyagarbha and others are not fit to be the locus of auspiciousness (*śubhāśraya*) because they are impure due to their connection with the three types of creative contemplation (*bhāvanā*); thus, their status as the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) is determined.

Furthermore, as for what has been said by some regarding the entire collection of words—consisting of injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and mantras—[it is argued that they all ultimately refer to him].
Validity must be described as consisting solely in the expression of an action (*kārya*).

Since it is impossible to determine a word’s power to convey meaning outside of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), and since linguistic usage is rooted in the cognition of an action, the meaning of a word is exclusively of the nature of an action.
A word is not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to an already established entity (*pariniṣpanna-vastu*).
To this it is replied:

Is this a royal decree that the capacity of words to convey meaning must be ascertained solely through the linguistic usage of sentences that prompt action? It is extremely easy to grasp the capacity of a word to convey meaning even with respect to established entities (*siddhavastu*).
