For instance, suppose someone is sent with the instruction, "Inform Devadatta by means of some hand gesture or the like that a staff is standing in the inner room. Engaged in making that known, he utters the words, "A staff is standing in the inner room.

A bystander who understands this hand gesture—though previously proficient in verbal communication—just as one who is mute might, employs the word "in the inner room" for the sake of communicating that same meaning.

Since we observe the use of the word "the staff is standing," one understands that this specific word is the signifier of this particular object; what difficulty is there in this? Likewise, when a child is gradually pointed toward various objects by his mother, father, and others using words such as "this is your father," "this is your mother," "this is your uncle," "this is a man," "this is a deer," "this is the moon," or "this is a snake," [he comes to understand the relationship between word and object].
Having been repeatedly instructed by those very words regarding those objects, and having observed the arising of his own cognition with respect to those objects,

he determines through a sequence of steps that the application of those words to those objects— preceded by pointing with a finger— is based on their capacity to convey meaning due to the absence of any other relation and because of the instruction of the person who established the convention; and then, once again, for him...
Having been instructed by previous elders that "this is the meaning of this word," one understands the meaning of all words and then employs every collection of sentences oneself.

In this very way, one comes to know that all words denote their own individual meanings, and that specific combinations [of words] express specific relations as they actually exist; thus, the insistence that linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) has only a functional purpose (*kāryārtha*) is [merely] a dogmatic restriction.

It is free from bondage; therefore, it is established that because the capacity of a word to convey its meaning regarding an object is ascertained, all Vedānta passages indeed convey Brahman—characterized as previously described, the cause of the entire universe and the source of all auspicious qualities. (117)

Moreover, let it be that linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) pertains solely to action (*kārya*). Even the sentences of the Vedānta teach everything as being useful for action alone, insofar as they present [liberation] as a fruit serving as a qualification for the person entitled to a specific action concerning meditation (*upāsanā*). This is just like [the mention of] heaven and so forth—which consists of a particular place unmixed with suffering—as a fruit; or like the "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhā*) in the Rātrisatra sacrifice; or like the relationship between the means and the end established by the threat of a hundred-fold torments for one who brandishes a staff against a Brahmin.

For instance, in the passage "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," the attainment of Brahman is heard as the fruit that serves as a qualification for the person entitled to the ritual act consisting of the meditation on Brahman.

Furthermore, in the passage "One desiring to attain the Supreme should know Brahman," the very nature of Brahman and all its attributes, which are perceived as the object to be attained, are established solely for the sake of utility toward that ritual act.

All that has been stated and all that has not been stated—such as its being the creator of the world, the destroyer, the substratum, the inner self, and so forth—is contained within that very [Brahman]; thus, nothing is untenable.
This being the case, all the meanings found in the mantras and arthavādas that are non-contradictory and unprecedented are established precisely as supplements to the injunctions (*vidhi*).

As it is said in the *Dramiḍabhāṣya*, beginning with the citation from scripture, "For one is indeed born with a debt," even though the passage is intended for the praise of the sacrificial portions (*avadāna*), nevertheless, praise is not possible for what does not exist.

This is what is meant: for every portion consisting of *arthavāda* (explanatory praise), by recounting thousands of unseen qualities of the sacrifice and its subsidiaries—which consist in the propitiation of a deity—as well as of the deity to be propitiated, produces a cognition of excellence (*prāśastya*) regarding the ritual act. If those qualities were non-existent, there would be no cognition of excellence at all; therefore, it is for the sake of producing a cognition of excellence in the ritual that the *arthavāda* makes known the actual existence of those qualities.
In this very manner, all matters understood through the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) of the mantras are established.
Furthermore, those who maintain that the meaning of a sentence consists in what is to be done (*kārya*) must state: what is this so-called "state of being to be done" (*kāryatva*)?
If it is argued that it is "being brought about by an agent's effort" (*kṛtibhāvabhāvitā*) and "being the objective of an agent's effort" (*kṛtyuddeśyatā*), [we respond as follows].
What is this "being the intended object of an action" (*kṛtyuddeśyatva*)?

If it is argued that "that with reference to which an action occurs is the being the intended object of an action," then what is this so-called "reference" (*adhikāra*) of an action whose nature is human effort (*puruṣavyāpāra*)?

If it is argued that "the state of being the objective of an effort (kṛtyuddeśyatva) is that which a person produces an effort for the desire to attain," then, alas, the state of being the objective of an effort is simply the state of being desired (iṣṭatva).
Now, if you think thus: "The desired object itself possesses two aspects:
its existence as the object of desire and its capacity to impel the person."

In this regard, the claim that the form of "impelling" (prerakatva) consists in being the intended object of an action is a futile exertion caused by dogmatic attachment to one's own position. For indeed, "impelling" is simply the fact that what is perceived as the object of a desire cannot be established without the arising of one's own effort;
it is from that alone that activity proceeds.

If it is understood that when a desire arises, the desired object cannot be accomplished without the production of one's own effort, then from that [understanding] the desire-to-act (*cikīrṣā*) arises, and subsequently the person proceeds to act; such is the process according to those who know the truth. Therefore, apart from the fact that the desired object acquires its existence through dependence on the action (*kṛti*), no other thing called "being the objective of the action" is observed. Now, it might be argued that the cause of desirability is its being favorable to the person.
If it is argued that being conducive to the person (*puruṣa*) means being the intended object of an action (*kṛti*),
this is not so;
for "being conducive to the person" and "pleasure" are not different in meaning.
Likewise, there is a category of suffering that is favorable to a person.
Therefore, it is impossible for anything other than pleasure to possess the quality of being favorable to a person.
But is it not observed that even the cessation of suffering, which is distinct from pleasure, possesses favorability to a person?
This is not so;
for the distinction between pleasure and pain is that pleasure is what is favorable to the self, while pain is what is unfavorable to the self.
In that regard, what is favorable to the self is accepted as pleasure.
That which is contrary to it is suffering and undesirable;
therefore, because the conjunction with suffering is unbearable, its cessation is also desired.
Precisely because of this equality in being desired, there arises the delusion that it is favorable.

For thus, there are three states for the transmigrating person (puruṣa) who is conjoined with primordial nature (prakṛti): conjunction with the favorable, conjunction with the unfavorable, and abiding in one's own essential nature (svarūpa).
Among these, the cessation of the connection with the unfavorable and the cessation of the connection with the favorable are simply abiding in one's own essential nature.
Therefore, while the connection with the unfavorable persists, even abiding in one's own essential nature—which consists in the cessation of that [unfavorable connection]—is desired.

In that case, because of the similarity in being desired, there arises the delusion that [the injunction] is favorable. (120) Therefore, since favorability consists in the nature of pleasure, the authorities ridicule those who claim that the injunction (*niyoga*) is favorable.

For it is precisely by way of turning one away from an undesired particular object that the injunction's status as an injunction, its stability, and its character as something not previously known (*apūrva*) are perceived.

In the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," the determination that the task (*kārya*) is a means to heaven arises precisely from its co-occurrence with the term "desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*), which establishes it as distinct from the mere action. Nor should it be argued that in the phrase "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), the mandate (*niyoga*) is first understood as being primary in itself, and that through its co-occurrence with the term "desiring heaven," the mandate is subsequently seen as conducive to the attainment of heaven for the sake of its own fulfillment.
For from the word "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), it is understood that the meaning of the verbal root is to be accomplished by human effort.

Precisely through its co-occurrence with the term "desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*), there arises the status of the *niyoga* (an injunction) as something distinct from the meaning of the verbal root, characterized by its stability and its being a *pūrva* (something not previously known).
And this [status] is the basis for the cognition that [the sacrifice] is a means to attain heaven.

The linguistic convention of the world—that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth denote an action that is a means to heaven, which is fit to be construed with the meaning of the word "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) uttered in proximity—is also disregarded. What is meant is this: immediately upon hearing a sentence consisting of a collection of words whose function is to express meanings already related (*anvitābhidhāyin*), that which is conveyed by one word is understood as being precisely that which is fit to be construed with the meanings expressed by the other words uttered in proximity.
And that [word] has the nature of being a means to heaven;
therefore, like an action (*kriyā*), its lack of subservience to any other purpose is also abandoned precisely because of contradiction.
For this very reason, in expressions such as "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā," the word *gaṅgā* is accepted as having the function of presenting an object suitable for the habitation of the hamlet.
Just as, when the word *gaṅgā* is first heard, the meaning of *gaṅgā* is recalled, and thus the drinkability of the word-meaning *gaṅgā* does not enter into the connection with the sentence-meaning;
so too here, upon hearing merely the word *yajeta*, the fact that the "task" (*kārya*) is recalled as having no other purpose does not persist at the time of its connection with the sentence-meaning.
Furthermore, the claim that "at the moment the word denoting the task is heard, the task is first perceived as having no other purpose" is also untenable.

At the time of learning [the meaning of words], the status of an action such as "bringing a cow" as something to be done (*kāryatā*) is understood precisely because it is a means to achieve a particular desired object, even though that action is of the nature of suffering.

Therefore, for one who asserts that an injunction (*niyoga*) is of the nature of pleasure and favorable to the person, the claim that an injunction is favorable to the person contradicts the experience of all people; furthermore, there is a contradiction with one's own experience.

Even in cases such as "one desiring rain should sacrifice with the Karīrī [offering]," although the injunction is established, the favorability of the injunction—distinct from the rain itself—is based on the fact that it is the cause for the accomplishment of the rain and so forth.
It is not experienced.

Even if there is no fixed rule regarding the attainment of rain and so forth in this life, nevertheless, precisely because of that lack of fixed rule, the accomplishment of the injunction must necessarily be accepted;
yet, in that case, the experience of pleasure—which is synonymous with favorability—is not observed.
Thus, according to the manner stated, no "being the object of an effort" (*kṛtyuddeśyatva*) is observed that exceeds "being desired as achievable through effort" (*kṛtisādhyeṣṭatva*).

If it is argued that "being the object of an effort" means "being the principal (*śeṣin*) with respect to the effort," then it must be explained: what is this "being the principal," and what is "being the subordinate" (*śeṣatva*)?
If it is argued that a *śeṣa* (subordinate) is that which is related to an action (*kārya*), and that being related to that [action] constitutes *śeṣitva* (the state of being the principal),
then in that case, it would follow that *śeṣitva* is nothing other than the state of being an action itself.
It is precisely the status of being an effect (*kāryatva*) that is being investigated.
If it is argued that "subsidiarity" (*śeṣatva*) consists in being fit for pervasion by an activity directed toward another,
then what is this so-called "being directed toward another"?
For this very point is being investigated:
if it is argued that "being the object of reference" (uddeśyatva) means "being desired" (īpsitatva) and "being that which is to be accomplished" (sādhyatva),
then what is this "being desired"?
If it is argued that [the purpose] consists in being the object of human effort (*kṛti*), then the very purpose for a person’s initiation of effort is indeed the purpose of that effort.
And since that [purpose] is the object of desire and its own acquisition depends upon effort, this is precisely what was stated previously.
For this alone constitutes the relationship of subordinate and principal (*śeṣa-śeṣibhāva*) in all cases.

That whose very nature consists in being something to be accepted (*upādeyatva*) through the desire to produce an excellence in another is the subordinate (*śeṣa*), while that [in whom the excellence is produced] is the supreme (*para*) or the principal (*śeṣin*).

The sacrifice and the like, as well as the effort directed toward them, possess the nature of being accepted through the desire for the production of a fruit; everything else is accepted through the desire for the accomplishment of the sacrifice and so forth. In the same way, even for those such as a slave born in the house (*garbhadāsa*), their very nature consists in being accepted through the production of an excellence in a particular person.

Thus, because everything—whether conscious or unconscious, eternal or non-eternal—is to be accepted [as an object] through the desire of the Lord to bestow excellence upon Himself, the very nature of every entity is that it exists solely as a subordinate (śeṣa) to the Lord; and since the Lord is the sovereign (śeṣin) of all, it is stated in such passages as: "He who controls all, He who rules over all, the Lord of the universe."
The claim that "that which is to be accomplished by human effort (*kṛti*) and is primary is designated as the 'task' (*kārya*)" is attractive only to those who possess blind faith.

Furthermore, in injunctions such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*), how can it be understood— contrary to the grammatical tradition— that words like "one desiring heaven," which are intended to provide the specific agent (*kartṛ*) expressed by the verbal suffix (*lakāra*), instead have the purpose of providing the specific person to be enjoined (*niyojya*)?
If it is argued that the connection of agency with one who is qualified by the heaven to be attained does not occur in the means to heaven, [we reply:

the connection of being the person to be enjoined (*niyojyatva*) likewise does not occur; for it is precisely the certainty regarding the status of being a means to heaven that establishes the connection of agency as proven by scripture.
Once that connection of agency is established by scripture, the certainty regarding its being a means to heaven is then produced.

Just as when it is said, "One who desires to eat should go to Devadatta’s house," the fact that the one desiring food possesses the agency (kartṛtva) regarding going to Devadatta’s house is heard [in the sentence] itself; thus, even though it was previously unknown, the fact that [going] is a means to eating is understood. The same applies here. It is not logical to assume the agency of something heard as the agent of one action in relation to another action; for instance, in the case of the injunction *yajeta* ("one should sacrifice"), the assumption of agency regarding the act of knowing (*viddhi*) is made for that which is heard as the agent of the sacrifice.
For the very conception of the intellect as an agent is what constitutes its status as the "one to be enjoined" (niyojya). As it has been said:
"The one to be enjoined is he who perceives every task as his own.
If it is argued that this state of being a perceiver conforms to the state of being a sacrificer (yaṣṭṛ), [we reply:]...

In the case of "Devadatta should cook," since Devadatta is heard as the agent (*kartṛ*) of the act of cooking, it is not logical to assume that his movement toward the purpose of cooking constitutes his agency in that movement. Furthermore, why is an "unseen force" (*apūrva*) postulated as the enduring form denoted by words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*)?
If you argue that it is because the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the word *svargakāma* ("one who desires heaven") would otherwise be untenable; [we reply: no.
What is the inconsistency here?
For one who desires heaven is indeed "one who desires heaven" (svargakāma).

If it is argued that for such a person desiring heaven, a ritual action such as sacrifice—which is momentary in its destruction—is incapable of accomplishing a heaven that arises at a later time; [then we reply:]
This is an untenable position for those who have not smelled the scent of the Vedantic tenets.
Those who know the Veda declare that the Supreme Lord, the Blessed Nārāyaṇa, when propitiated by all ritual actions, bestows each respective desired fruit.

As the Draviḍācārya, the foremost among the knowers of the Veda, has said: "For, with the desire to share in the fruit, they seek to please the Self through ritual actions; being pleased, He is sufficient for the fruit—such is the established limit of the scripture."

Desiring a connection with the fruits [of action], they seek to propitiate through rituals such as sacrifice, giving, and oblation the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva— the Supreme Self denoted by words such as Indra— who exists as the respective inner controller (antaryāmin) of the senses and other faculties via those deities;
for it is He, when propitiated by rituals, who bestows upon them the desired fruits— this is the meaning.
And thus says the Śruti: "The navel of the world sustains the universe—the performed and the offered, the manifold, that which has been born and that which is being born.
By "the performed and the offered" (iṣṭāpūrta), all action enjoined by the Śruti and Smṛti is meant.

He sustains that entire universe; the Supreme Person, abiding as the inner self within each of those [beings] through whom the [sacrifices] appear to be connected with all the deities such as Indra, Agni, and Varuṇa, sustains it Himself alone.
Thus he accepts [the title].

He is the "navel of the world" (*bhuvanasya nābhiḥ*): the sustainer of the world—which is filled with all castes, beginning with Brahmins and Kṣatriyas—and when propitiated by various actions, he is called the "navel" because he sustains the worlds by bestowing their respective desired fruits.

He says that this very Self is indeed what is denoted by those various terms, because it is the inner self of other deities such as Fire and Wind, in the words: "That alone is fire, that is wind, that is the sun, and that is the moon.
As it was said by the Blessed One:
"Whatever form of deity a devotee desires to worship with faith..."
Whatever firm faith he possesses, that very same faith I establish for him.
"Endowed with faith in Him, he strives for His propitiation;
and from Him he obtains his desires, which are here ordained by Me alone.

(Gītā 7.22) Regarding the phrase "whichever form," the meaning is that these are the forms or bodies of the Blessed Lord who exists as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of specific deities such as Indra and others.
"For I am indeed the enjoyer and also the Lord of all sacrifices," and so forth. "And also the Lord" means the giver of all fruits.
And as you are constantly worshipped by sacrifices, O Acyuta, who consists of all the gods.
O Protector, those men who, devoted to their own duty, have honored you,
cross over this entire illusion for the sake of their own liberation.
Thus, it is explained throughout all the Vedas, including the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, that all ritual acts are essentially forms of worship to the Lord of All;
and that the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), propitiated by those various acts, bestows the respective fruits desired by the performer.

For in this way, the Blessed One—who is omnipotent, omniscient, and the Lord of All—is the enjoyer of all rites such as sacrifice, gift-giving, and oblation prescribed in the Vedas, acting through His form as the inner controller (antaryāmin) of deities such as Indra, and the giver of all fruits.
And all the Śrutis declare him to be the giver, beginning with:
"Wherein the four Hotṛ-priests attain perfection along with the gods," and so forth.
The "four Hotṛs" are the sacrifices.
In that Supreme Self who exists as the inner controller (antaryāmin) within the gods,
the sacrifices "attain union with the gods"— meaning they enter into a relationship with the gods.

What is being stated is that Indra and the other deities, who exist as the bodies of the Supreme Self abiding in the form of the inner controller, possess a connection with the sacrifices and so forth.
As it was said by the Blessed One:
"The enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the Great Lord of all the worlds.
Therefore, all ritual actions are essentially forms of worship directed toward the Supreme Person, who is the inner self of the deities such as Agni and others.

Since that very [action] is the bestower of the desired fruit, what purpose is served here by postulating an *apūrva* (unseen force) which lies far outside the path of linguistic derivation, whether as something denoted or as something merely imagined?
This being the case, what meaning is actually embraced by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and the like?

Since the root-meaning—such as sacrifice, which consists of acts like worship directed toward a deity—is established through linguistic derivation as being achievable through the agent’s activity, there is nothing inconsistent in the optative suffixes expressing this very fact.
For suffixes denoting an agent, that which is to be expressed is indeed the manner in which the meaning of the verbal root is related to the agent's activity.
Others say this [manner] consists of [tenses such as] the past or present;
however, the optative (*liṅ*) and other such suffixes express the state of being to be accomplished through the agent's activity. (125)

Moreover, the very injunctions for various rites—which enjoin action as something to be performed by those desiring [results]—declare that action consists in the propitiation of a deity and that the attainment of results occurs through that means, such as:
"One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu; Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity; he approaches Vāyu with his own share; he (Vāyu) leads him to prosperity," and so forth.

Since no inconsistency whatsoever is observed here regarding the accomplishment of the result, the claim that the understanding of action as a means to a result is derived from the *upādāna* (the material cause or the act of taking up the means) is also untenable.

The meaning is that the supplementary portion of the passage (*vākyaśeṣa*) itself makes known the manner in which sacrifice and the like are the means to a result, as required by the injunction. Therefore, in the case of the statement "one should not threaten a Brahmin," it is accepted that the fact that threatening— the object of the prohibition— is a means to a hundred-fold torture, as heard in the supplementary portion of the sentence dedicated to the injunction prohibiting threatening, is indeed useful for the prohibitory injunction.

Furthermore, in this case, why is the fact that sacrifices and the like are means to a result postulated by means of "appropriation" (upādāna), while disregarding the manner in which those very sacrifices are understood from the supplementary passages (vākyaśeṣa) to be means for attaining desirable ends such as heaven—which are enjoined as things to be performed by those desiring [those ends]?
It is heard that after depositing a treasure of gold in a room, a miserly person greedy for *kodrava* grain begs of others; this very thing is seen among you.
Even the state of being the means for hundreds of torments does not occur through the medium of the unseen (adṛṣṭa).
For one who performs what is enjoined, fails to perform what is prescribed, and performs what is censured—all pleasures and pains arise solely from the grace and the restraint of the Supreme Person.

For it is He alone who causes bliss; thus he becomes one who has attained fearlessness; yet for him there is fear, for out of fear of Him the wind blows, out of fear the sun rises, and out of fear of Him both fire and moon shine.
"Death runs as the fifth.

By the command of this Imperishable One, O Gārgī, the sun and the moon stand held apart; by the command of this Imperishable One, O Gārgī, humans praise one who gives, the gods [praise] the sacrificer, and the ancestors [praise] the sacrificial ladle.

There are many such scriptural passages, beginning with "dependent upon Him," as stated in the Dramiḍa-bhāṣya: "By His command the wind blows, the rivers flow, and by Him the reservoirs of water have their boundaries fixed; like rams, they bellow together.
Indeed, bound by His volition, these things in the world neither fall nor burst apart.
Having recognized those who follow his own teaching, that wise Blessed One, out of compassion, causes them to prosper, thinking, "They are skillful in action.

For those who perform the prescribed rites—such as meditation preceded by knowledge of the true nature of the Supreme Person—there arise, through his grace, happiness culminating in the attainment of him and fearlessness, according to their respective capacities. (126)

For one who does not perform the prescribed actions— such as worship and the like— which are preceded by that knowledge, and who instead performs censurable acts, there arise, precisely through the restraint [of the Lord], immeasurable sufferings preceded by the failure to attain that [state] and fear,
as stated by the Blessed One: "Perform action with constancy, for action is indeed superior to inaction."
Having thus prescribed that all action must be performed preceded by knowledge,
and having established that all action is for the sake of worshipping Me and that all beings are subject to My control, [He says: "having renounced all actions in Me."
Those men who constantly follow this teaching of mine,
full of faith and free from carping, they too are liberated from the bonds of action.
But those who, finding fault with this, do not follow my teaching—
know them to be deluded in all knowledge, lost, and devoid of discernment.

Thus, having praised those who follow their own command and censured those who act contrary to it, and having further declared that those who do not observe their own command fall into the nature of the Asuras, the lowest state has been described: "Those cruel haters of Me, the lowest of men among all transmigrating beings, the inauspicious— I perpetually cast into the very wombs of the Asuras."
"Having entered the womb of an asura, deluded birth after birth, they fail to reach Me, O son of Kuntī, and from there they go to the lowest state. Thus [it is said].
"Even while constantly performing all actions, one who has Me as his refuge..."
By my grace, one attains the eternal and imperishable state.
And thus, the eternal state has been declared for those who follow their own [inner] command.

In the *Devatādhikaraṇa*, hyperbolic statements were made so that those who have not heard the Vedānta might not lack faith in ritual action; the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the knowers of the Veda is that all [scriptures] constitute a single teaching, so that there may be faith in mere action.
Of this very Supreme Brahman...

Like the nature of Nārāyaṇa—which consists of immeasurable knowledge, bliss, and purity—He possesses infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable auspicious qualities such as knowledge, power, strength, sovereignty, valor, and splendor; He is the one who sets in motion the entire multitude of all sentient and insentient entities other than Himself by His own volition; He possesses a divine form of a single, uniform nature that accords with His own will and is suited to Him; He is endowed with various, unsurpassed, and infinite auspicious ornaments appropriate to that form; He wields diverse, infinite, and wonderful weapons of immeasurable variety that correspond to His own power; He is accompanied by a consort whose majesty is of infinite greatness, possessing a nature, qualities, glory, sovereignty, character, and so forth that accord with His own and who is endowed with immeasurable virtues such as knowledge and action; He is surrounded by an infinite retinue of attendants whose number is beyond measure and who possess auspicious qualities corresponding to His own; He possesses an infinite great majesty consisting of all objects of enjoyment, instruments of enjoyment, and the like, which are appropriate to Him; and He is the object of the scope of speech and mind regarding His divine abode, eternal nature, and stainless character.
And there are thousands of scriptural passages [to this effect]:
"I know this great Puruṣa, resplendent like the sun, beyond darkness;
he who is this golden Puruṣa within the sun."
His eyes are like a white lotus with reddish corners.

Within that space which is inside the heart, there is this person (*puruṣa*) consisting of mind (*manomaya*), immortal, and golden. "Consisting of mind" means he is apprehended by the pure mind alone. From this person, the lightning-like moments of consciousness were born.

The meaning is "from the person who has the color of lightning. Like a streak of lightning situated within a dark cloud, shining brightly, this very crest of flame residing in the space within the small lotus—having the nature of the Supreme Self which possesses the luster of a dark cloud contained within itself—shines like lightning with a dark cloud contained within it. This is the meaning.
He consists of mind, has the vital breath as his body, and has light as his form. His desires are true, his resolves are true.

He has space as his self; he possesses all desires, he is all desires, he possesses all odors, he possesses all tastes. He has encompassed all this, and is free from speech and free from heedlessness.
"Her garments are of mahārajana," and so forth;
she is the sovereign of this world, the consort of Viṣṇu;
Hrī and Lakṣmī are her two wives.
The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu,
which dwells beyond this realm,
which is one, unmanifest, of infinite forms, the ancient universe, situated beyond darkness.
He who knows [Brahman] hidden in the secret cave, in the highest heaven;
he who is its supervisor in the highest heaven— that indeed is that, and it is yet to be.
This is that [state] in the imperishable, supreme heaven; this meaning is established by hundreds of scriptural passages beginning with these words.

From the statement, "The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu," it is understood that there exist certain individuals who possess complete knowledge and perceive [it] at all times. (128) Viṣṇu’s supreme abode refers to the supreme state of Viṣṇu, the Supreme Brahman. Because of the expression "the wise ever behold," it is known that there are some who possess vision at every moment and are endowed with perfect wisdom.
The grammatical formulation is either "those who are wise always see," or "those who always see are wise.
If it is argued that in both cases a manifold injunction is not possible, we say: no.

Because everything has not been previously established, the supreme state, distinguished by all its qualities, is enjoined. As it has been said: "Those qualities should be enjoined because of their non-separation from the purpose of the injunction, provided they have not been taught by another.

Just as in the injunction of a ritual action such as "The cake on eight potsherds for Agni," since neither the action nor its qualities have been previously established, [the rite] is characterized by all its qualities.

In the same way, ritual action is prescribed here as well; for the wise always maintain that there is no contradiction, since [the scripture] establishes that Viṣṇu’s supreme abode has not been attained by virtue of being visible.

Furthermore, the instrumental mantras—which are descriptive of the action being performed, take the form of hymns (*stotra*) and recitations (*śastra*), and are employed in rites such as silent chanting (*japa*)—are those recited within the specific context (*prakaraṇa*).

For the Vaidikas maintain that all [Vedic texts], whether recited in a specific context or not, inform one of their own meaning exactly as it exists— unattained yet non-contradictory— just like a Brāhmaṇa.
A *stotra* is that which brings about the identification (*abhimāna*) of a quality and its possessor through a chanted mantra.
The *śastra* is the designation of qualities residing in a substratum (the qualified entity) by means of mantras that are not chanted (*apragīta*).

Furthermore, the manifestation of a specific meaning assigned [to a mantra], which establishes particular qualities—such as those pertaining to deities—that are neither unestablished nor contradictory, is indeed consistent with its ritual application (*viniyoga*).
This scriptural statement (*śruti*) does not have liberated beings as its object.
For it is impossible for them [the liberated souls] to perceive [Brahman] at all times;
nor does it have as its object a continuous stream of liberated beings,
because the scripture would be contradicted by the fact that it is understood as having each individual agent as its perceiver, based on the expression "they always see."
It has been stated that meanings found in mantras and explanatory passages (arthavādas) are established even when those texts have a purpose directed toward action (*kāryaparatva*).
How much more so, then, is it established that the intention (*tātparya*) is directed toward an already established entity (*siddhavastu*), whereby all [the scriptural teachings] become coherent?
Now, one might object: here, in the phrase "that supreme abode of Viṣṇu," it is the very nature of the Supreme (*parasvarūpa*) itself that is denoted by the term "supreme abode" (*paramapada*).
Because in such passages as "the supreme state called Viṣṇu, free from all that is to be abandoned," non-difference is observed; [we reply:
this is not so, for [it says] "he who dwells beyond the reach of this world."

In such passages as "That [is] in the Imperishable, in the highest heaven," "He who is its supervisor in the highest heaven," and "He who knows [it] hidden in the cave in the highest heaven," there is the perception of the supreme abode alone.

And because of the indication of distinction in the phrase "that supreme abode of Viṣṇu," it is understood from that very [text]—by the qualification "the supreme abode named Viṣṇu"—that there exists another supreme abode as well. This supreme station is described by the wise as being eternally visible. (129)

This is what is meant: in some instances, the state of another (the liberated soul) is denoted by the term "supreme abode" (paramapada); in others, it is the essential nature of the self as dissociated from primordial matter (prakṛti); and in others, it is the essential nature of the Lord (Bhagavat).
"The wise always behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu"—thus [is described] the transcendent station.

At the times of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, [the power] proceeds in a threefold manner through the activity of the qualities (guṇas); yet His supreme state is beyond the qualities (aguṇa) and great.
In this [verse], the nature of the Self as dissociated from primordial matter (prakṛti) is described;
and in the passage, "The supreme state called Viṣṇu, free from all that is to be abandoned," the essential nature of the Blessed Lord is described.
All three of these are designated by the term "supreme state" (*paramapada*) because they constitute the ultimate attainment.
If it is asked how all three possess the quality of being the supreme attainment, [the answer is]:
the essential nature of the Blessed One (*bhagavat-svarūpa*) is the supreme state precisely because it is the supreme attainment.
The two other [states] are also the supreme state precisely because they have the attainment of the Blessed One as their core.
The attainment of one’s own true nature, which is liberated from the bondage of all karma, has the attainment of the Blessed One as its core.

In the passage, "These are the true desires, covered by the untrue," one's own karma is indicated by the word "untrue" (*anṛta*) because it serves to conceal the multitude of the Blessed One's qualities. (130)
If it is asked how it is understood that the concealment of the form of reality is the karma of the *kṣetrajña*, [the answer is:
"O King, another power called ignorance (*avidyā*) is accepted as a third;
it is all-pervading, O King, and it envelops the power of the *kṣetrajña*."
"Because of being obscured by that [ignorance], one experiences all the extremely continuous torments of saṃsāra," according to such scriptural statements. (131)
It is quite clear that even the attainment of the supreme state has the attainment of the Blessed One as its very core.

In the phrase "dwelling beyond this dust" (*kṣayantam asya rajasaḥ parāke*), the word *rajas* refers to primordial nature (*prakṛti*) consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇātmikā*), because pure *rajas* alone cannot persist independently.
The meaning is: dwelling—that is, residing—in that station which stands having transcended this primordial nature composed of the three qualities.
By this, it is understood that Viṣṇu’s abode is beyond the object consisting of the three guṇas which serves as the experience of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
In the verse, "I know this Great Puruṣa, resplendent like the sun, beyond darkness," the word "darkness" (tamas) likewise refers to that very primordial nature (prakṛti).

Because darkness alone cannot endure, and because this [verse] forms a single syntactical unit with the phrase "dwelling beyond the rajas," the meaning understood is: "I know that Great Person, resplendent like the sun, who dwells beyond darkness.
This is the Brahman that is truth, knowledge, and infinite.

"He who knows that which is hidden in the secret cave, in the highest heaven (*parama-vyoman*); that [is] in the imperishable (*akṣara*), in the highest heaven"—from this it is understood that the place is of an unchanging nature and is designated by the term "highest heaven.

Since the imperishability of that eternal place is heard in the phrase "in the imperishable, in the highest heaven," the perishable forms such as the solar orb and so forth are not what is designated by the term "highest heaven."
In passages such as "Where the ancient Sādhyas, the gods, abide,

where the ṛṣis are who were first-born in the beginning," and so forth, it is understood that they alone are the "wise ones" (sūrayaḥ). Likewise, in the verse, "The wise, the eloquent, the ever-watchful kindle that which is the highest step of Viṣṇu," the term "viprāsaḥ" refers to those possessed of intelligence.
The word *vipanyavaḥ* means those whose nature is to praise;

*jāgṛvāṃsaḥ* means those whose knowledge is unerring—indeed, it is precisely because their knowledge is unerring that they mean those who always praise that supreme abode of Viṣṇu and kindle [the fire of meditation]; this is the meaning.

For these [qualities], such as retinue, abodes, and so forth, are included within the very nature of the Supreme Brahman—which, as stated in the passage "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone"—possesses a multitude of auspicious qualities such as knowledge, power, and sovereignty.
From the statement "Being alone, indeed, was this in the beginning, one only, without a second," the inclusion of these [qualities] within Brahman is understood;

for they too are but a portion of its auspicious attributes. Furthermore, because in the passage "Being alone, my dear, was this in the beginning," the word "this" (*idam*) refers to the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of the elements to be enjoyed, the class of enjoyers subject to karma, and their mixture, the wise perceive [Brahman] as Being.
Thus, by virtue of being eternally manifest, they are not included among those subject to karma.

From the words "free from evil" (*apahatapāpman*) up to "free from thirst" (*apipāsa*), all that is of the nature of the rejectable—pertaining to the three *guṇas* of *prakṛti*, the products of *prakṛti*, and the *puruṣa* in conjunction with them—is negated; then, by the phrase "whose desires are true" (*satyakāma*), [the text establishes] the collection of objects of enjoyment and the instruments of enjoyment for his own experience.
The truthfulness of everything has been established.
He whose desires are unreal is "one whose desires are true" (satyakāma).
Desires are so called because they are desired.

The meaning is that by that Supreme Brahman, those objects of enjoyment, their accessories, and so forth, which are desired according to His own will, are real and eternal. Although other things serving as instruments for His sport (*līlā*) may also be capable of being related to valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), they are unstable because they are subject to modification; therefore, their opposite—stability—is expressed by the word "real" (*satya*).

Thus, while these objects of enjoyment, their accessories, and so forth are eternal, unsurpassed, and infinite, even the accomplishment of unprecedented and immeasurable purposes occurs through mere volition (*saṃkalpa*) alone. This is what is meant by the phrase "of true resolve" (*satyasaṃkalpa*).
He speaks thus:

"Of all these objects of enjoyment and instruments of play—whether sentient or insentient, stable or unstable—their very nature, their persistence, their activity, and their various distinctions are entirely dependent upon his volition;
therefore, he is called 'one whose volition is true'. (133)
This matter is also stated in the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*, which serve as supplements to the Vedas:
"Seeing that those two were intelligent and well-versed in the Vedas,
the Lord had them master the purpose of supplementing the Vedas."
Thus, in the glorious Rāmāyaṇa, which was composed as an expansion of the Vedas,
it is clearly stated: "This great yogi is the eternal Supreme Self,
without beginning, middle, or end, greater than the great, the most supreme."
The Sustainer beyond darkness, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace;
marked with the Śrīvatsa on his chest, eternally glorious, unconquerable, everlasting, and immutable.
Various kinds of arrows, as well as bows of great length,
all followed the descendant of Kakutstha, assuming human forms.
He entered the Vaiṣṇava splendor together with his body and his followers.
O King, in that glorious Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa, all these powers are established;
that is the final, great form of Hari, which possesses the nature of the entire universe.
O highly fortunate one, Hari is the embodied Brahman, consisting of all Brahman.
This Śrī, the mother of the world, is eternal and inseparable from Viṣṇu;
O best of the twice-born, as Viṣṇu is omnipresent, so too is she.
In the state of divinity she possesses a divine body, and in the state of humanity she is human;
indeed, she fashions her own form in accordance with the body of Viṣṇu.
For those yogins who are single-mindedly devoted and always meditate upon Brahman,
that supreme abode belongs to them which the wise indeed behold.
And time, consisting of units such as *kalās* and *muhūrtas*, is not the cause of transformation for that which is His manifestation.
And in the Mahābhārata: "The divine station is ageless, immeasurable, difficult to discern, accessible through the scriptures, and primordial."
Go, O Lord, and protect us who have sought refuge in you, being born in your own form in age after age.
"Time ripens there; indeed, Time is not the master there.
Thus [it is said]. And the author of the Sūtras speaks of the Supreme Brahman’s possession of form in the sūtra: "Because its qualities are taught as being within" (BS 1.1.20).
That which exists within the solar orb, possessing the luster of a great mountain of molten gold, and emitting hundreds of thousands of rays like the sun—[is that Brahman].

His long eyes were as pure as the petals of a white lotus that has blossomed with its well-polished stalk emerging from deep waters; he possessed beautiful eyebrows, a forehead, and a nose, with lips like coral and a lovely smile; his cheeks were radiant and soft, his neck was shaped like a conch shell, and from his high shoulders hung lovely divine ear-lobes like tender sprouts;
his arms were thick, rounded, and long, adorned with hands of exquisite copper hue and reddened fingers; his waist was slender and his chest broad.
With all his limbs perfectly proportioned, he possessed an indescribable divine form and a compact, smooth complexion; his pair of feet were as beautiful as blossomed white lotuses.

He wore yellow garments suited to his own nature and was adorned with infinite, wondrous, and endless divine ornaments such as a stainless crown, earrings, necklaces, the Kaustubha gem, armlets, bracelets, anklets, a waist-band, and others.
Adorned with the conch, discus, mace, sword, the Śrīvatsa mark, and a forest garland, he captivated the entire range of the minds and eyes of all beings with his limitless and unsurpassed beauty.

The Supreme Person is seen, who has filled the entire multitude of moving and non-moving beings with the nectar of his loveliness; who possesses most wonderful, inconceivable, and eternal youth; who is as delicate as a flower-blossom; who perfumes the infinite reaches of the quarters with the fragrance of his merit; whose profound majesty is intent upon traversing the three worlds; and whose subjects are graced by the glances of his eyes, sweet with compassion and affection.

And He is understood to be the Supreme Self, the Supreme Brahman, Nārāyaṇa—whose play consists in the arising, flourishing, and dissolution of the entire universe; who has cast off everything that is to be abandoned; who is a treasure-house of the multitude of all auspicious qualities; and who is distinct from all other entities. This is known because of the teaching of His attributes, as seen in such passages as: "He rules over all these worlds," "He rules over all desires," and "He has risen above all evils."

These are His qualities: "He is the controller of all, the lord of all, free from evil, ageless," and so forth, ending with "whose resolve is true"; as well as those qualities established by such scriptural passages as "Nārāyaṇa, Hari, the supreme, eternal, and beyond the universe; the Lord of the universe, the Self and Master of all.

(135) And the authors of the *Vākya* have explained all this very clearly through such statements as: "The golden person is seen"—this must be the conscious one who is within all, because of the teaching regarding the lordship over the worlds and desires, and likewise because of the rising [of the sun] and the destruction of evils, and so on.

And the impermanence and other such qualities of that form would have been refuted by the author of the Sūtras themselves; for, having established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that "that form is created for the sake of favoring [devotees], because it is due to the sovereignty of the conscious beings," and that "the collection of forms of the Supreme Person is for the sake of favoring the worshiper," [the Sūtra] states:
"Or rather, the form is supersensuous and perceived by the internal organ, because of the mention thereof."

Just as knowledge and other attributes are qualities constituting the very nature of the Supreme Brahman because they are designated as its essential form, so too this "form" (rūpa) is of the nature of His essence because it is designated by the Śruti as such.

This has been explained by the Commentator [Śaṅkara] as follows: "This is indeed the form of the Creator of the universe; however, it is not perceivable by the eye, but is grasped by the mind when it is unpolluted and possesses the necessary means [of purification], for the Śruti declares: 'It is not grasped by the eye, nor even by speech, but by the purified mind.'"
For the form of the deity is not taught as being material;

for the scripture speaks according to reality. Moreover, because of the reference in another context—beginning with "I know this great Puruṣa, sun-colored, beyond darkness," and "golden"—it refers to the Witness and so forth.
Because of the commonality of form, as in the case of "moon-face," the suffix *mayaṭ* is not employed here to denote a modification, since the self (*ātman*) is not something that can be produced.

Just as it is understood that the Supreme Brahman is distinguished by an immeasurable multitude of auspicious qualities from the description of the succession of excellent attributes such as knowledge and so forth, even so, from the description beginning with "the Person of solar hue," it is known that Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person who is the Supreme Brahman, possesses a most auspicious form that is self-conceived and corresponds to Himself.

Likewise, from the scriptural passage beginning, "Thus his sovereignty over the world; Hri and Lakshmi are the wives of Vishnu; the wise ever behold Him dwelling beyond darkness, far away from this region," it is understood that His wives, retinue, abode, and so forth exist exactly as described therein, because of such specific indications.
As the author of the Bhāṣya has said: "For the scripture speaks of things as they truly are.

What is meant by this is that, because of the scriptural declaration, "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite," the nature of the Supreme Self is distinct from everything else, being the opposite of all that is to be rejected, characterized by absolute, infinite, and exclusive unity, and by its own indivisibility.

Likewise, from such scriptural indications as, "He who is all-knowing and all-perceiving," "His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold," and "His knowledge, strength, and action are inherent; everything shines only after Him has shone; by His light all this is illumined," there exist unsurpassed and innumerable qualities that are distinct from both the manifest and the unmanifest.

Thus, from such designations as "having the color of the sun" and so forth, [the Lord's] form, retinue, abode, and other attributes are entirely distinct from all others; they are His own unique, uncommon qualities, whose essential nature and character are indescribable.

(137) If the Vedas are authoritative, then everything contained within their injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and mantras—namely, the entire range of unprecedented and non-contradictory matters—makes known the state of things exactly as they are.
Furthermore, the authority of the Vedas has been established by the statement: "The relationship between a word and its meaning is innate."
Just as fire, water, and so forth possess their powers of heat and so on by nature,
and just as the sense organs such as the eye possess the inherent power to produce specific cognitions, so too the word possesses an inherent power to convey meaning.
Nor can it be said that the word's capacity to convey meaning is rooted in convention, like the gestures of the hands and so forth.
Even though the continuity of beginningless tradition remains uninterrupted, because there is no knowledge of a person who established the convention,
all those things rooted in convention are known either directly or through a lineage;
nor is it appropriate to assume [a creator] as one would in the case of words such as "Devadatta."
And in those cases, the convention is known either directly or through a lineage.

However, in the case of words such as "cow" (*go*), even though there has been an uninterrupted succession since time immemorial, their power to convey meaning is inherent, precisely because the convention is not [newly] established.
Therefore, just like the burning power of fire and other elements, or the power of the sense faculties to cognize, the power of a word to convey meaning must also be accepted as inherent. (138)

[Objection: But surely, if the capacity to convey meaning belongs to a word by its very nature—just as it does to the sense organs—why does it require the apprehension of a relationship for that conveying power, [as if it were] like a logical mark (*liṅga*) and so forth? [Reply: It is said: Just as smoke and the like, when their necessary connection is known, produce the cognition of fire and the like, so too a word, when its necessary connection is known, produces the cognition of a specific object.
[Objection: If that is so, then the word would also be a logical mark (*liṅga*) of the specific object, and thus [the process] would be an inference (*anumāna*). [Reply: It is not so.

The relationship between word and meaning is precisely that of the signified and the signifier (*bodhya-bodhaka-bhāva*), whereas the relationship of smoke and so forth is of a different kind; thus, the distinction is that the latter produces cognition by way of [the cognition of] that relationship. Since it is observed that a word functions as a signifier only when its relationship [to the meaning] has been grasped, it is determined that even though the continuity of beginningless tradition is uninterrupted, the power of signification exists solely through the knowledge of the convention (*saṃketa*). (139)

Thus, those collections of words (*padasaṃghāta*) which convey a specific relation and are designated by the term "sentence" (*vākya*), where the sequence of their utterance is preceded by human intelligence, are called "human" (*pauruṣeya*) words. However,
where that sequence of utterance is always preceded by impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by preceding sequences of utterance, they are called "non-human" (*apauruṣeya*), and these are the Vedas.

This indeed is the authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatva*) and eternality (*nityatva*) of the Vedas: that they are uttered in that very same specific sequence by means of remembering that same particular order through the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by a previous utterance. And those collections of syllables established in a specific succession—the Vedas, divided into the branches of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, *Sāman*, and *Atharva*, existing in infinite recensions—are of the nature of injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and mantras. These Vedas reveal the essential nature of Nārāyaṇa, who is the Supreme Brahman, as well as the specific fruits resulting from the modes of worshipping Him.
The collection of words known as the Vedas, which reveal the nature of the Supreme Person, the means of His worship, and the fruits thereof, is indeed eternal.

Because the Vedas are infinite and difficult to fathom, the supreme sages, directed by the Supreme Person, have composed in every kalpa the Dharmaśāstras and the Itihāsas and Purāṇas— rooted in injunctions (vidhi), explanatory passages (arthavāda), and mantras— for the benefit of the entire world, having recollected the meaning of the Vedas.
And worldly words, having been extracted from the mass of the Vedas, are employed—just as before—as names for various specific objects and are used through traditional succession.

[Objection: But if all expressive words are indeed Vedic, then how is a difference in grammatical rules (lakṣaṇabheda)—such as "it is thus in the Veda" and "it is thus in the spoken language"—possible? [Reply:
It is said: it is the very same words, occurring in that same sequence, which are employed in that very manner.
There is no fault whatsoever in [interpreting] those [passages] as being applied otherwise;

for thus, Nārāyaṇa—who is known through the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs augmented by the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and Dharmaśāstras; who is the Supreme Brahman; who is the adversary of all that is to be rejected;

who is distinct from everything else; whose sole nature consists of unlimited knowledge and bliss; and who is a mine of an inherent, infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable multitude of auspicious qualities—is [the subject].

It has been established that [the Lord] is the source of the multitude of sentient and insentient entities whose forms, states of existence, and activities conform to His own volition; He possesses infinite great majesty whose essential nature and attributes are unfathomable; and He is the instrument for the play (*līlā*) of the manifold and infinite phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of various sentient and insentient beings.
Indeed, all this is Brahman; all this has its self in Him; "That Thou Art," O Śvetaketu.
Some call him Agni, others the Maruts, others Prajāpati;
some Indra, others Prāṇa, and still others the eternal Brahman.
The luminaries that are white in the world, the three worlds, the guardians of the worlds, the triple Veda,
the three sacrificial fires, and the five oblations— all these gods are indeed the Son of Devakī.
You are the sacrifice, you are the *vaṣaṭ* call, you are the *oṃ* syllable, O scorcher of foes;
you are the light of the seasons, the primordial Vasu among the Vasus, and you are Prajāpati.
The entire world is your body; the surface of the earth is your stability;
fire is your anger; the moon is your grace, O you who bear the Śrīvatsa mark.
The luminaries are Viṣṇu, the worlds are Viṣṇu, the forests, the mountains, and the quarters are Viṣṇu;
the rivers and the oceans—all that exists and all that does not exist, O best of brahmins, is he alone.

It has been stated that in such applications of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), Brahman alone is denoted in every way by all words, as being the body of all. The Supreme Brahman, whose resolve is true, having itself resolved, "May I become manifold," divided its own self—which had previously dissolved within itself—into the subtle primordial elements (*mahābhūta*) constituting the aggregate of non-conscious matter (*acit-samaṣṭi*) and the collection of the group of enjoyers (*bhoktṛ-varga*). From those subtle elements as a real substrate...

Having created the great elements and having entered into them as the essence of the class of enjoyers, and having fashioned the entire world with those great elements presided over by consciousness and mutually combined, He Himself also enters as the self of all and remains as the Supreme Self,
abiding in many ways within the body of all.
That which is this subtle substance of the great elements (mahābhūta) is designated by the term *prakṛti*;
and the aggregate of the group of enjoyers (*bhoktṛ*) alone is called by the term *puruṣa*.
Both that *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* exist as modes of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), being the body of the Supreme Self.
That very Supreme Self, who is the source of those [states], is designated by the terms *prakṛti* (primordial nature) and *puruṣa* (spirit).

"He desired: 'May I become many; may I procreate. Having created that, He entered into it. Having entered it, He became the manifest (*sat*) and the unmanifest (*tyat*), the defined (*nirukta*) and the undefined (*anirukta*), the supported (*nilayana*) and the unsupported (*anilayana*), and the conscious (*vijñāna*) and the unconscious (*avijñāna*)."
And that "both truth and falsehood became truth," as previously stated, is made clear by this very Śruti passage. Furthermore,

it has been stated that the means for attaining Brahman is supreme devotion (*parabhakti*)— which consists of meditative contemplation (*anudhyāna*) that has reached the state of most intense, direct perception, being exceedingly dear, and accomplished through steadfastness in devotion supported by one's own duties, preceded by the knowledge of reality acquired from the scriptures.

And the word *bhakti* (devotion) occurs in the sense of a specific kind of affection (*prīti*). Affection, moreover, is nothing other than a specific kind of knowledge. Now, one might object that "pleasure" (*sukha*) and "affection" (*prīti*) are not different in meaning.
For worldly people indeed hold that pleasure (*sukha*) is a distinct entity (*padārthāntara*) to be accomplished by a particular cognition (*jñānaviśeṣa*).
This is not so;
for that very particular cognition by which it is said to be accomplished is itself the pleasure. (142)
This is what is meant: cognitions of objects are common to pleasure, pain, and neutrality;
and they become such as they are through specific qualities dependent upon the objects.
That cognition which, being qualified by a particular object, is intended to be the producer of pleasure—that very cognition having that object is itself pleasure.
No other distinct category of entity (padārtha) is perceived beyond that [pleasure],
for the conventional usage of "being happy" is established by that alone.
Furthermore, the quality of being a differentiator for the knowledge of the nature of such pleasure belongs to an entity distinct from Brahman, which is characterized by gradation and instability.
But for Brahman, it is unlimitedly unsurpassed and stable;
thus it is said that "Brahman is bliss.
Since knowledge is dependent upon objects, [ordinary] bliss consists in the nature of pleasure; therefore, Brahman alone is bliss.

This is what [the scripture] says: "He is indeed rasa; for having obtained rasa, one becomes blissful. This means that Brahman itself is bliss; having obtained Brahman, one becomes happy. The Supreme Person, being Himself of infinite and unsurpassed bliss by His very nature, is the bliss of others as well, because there is no difference in His being the very essence of bliss.
The meaning is that he for whom Brahman becomes the object of knowledge becomes happy.
Thus, because the Supreme Brahman—the mine of an infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable multitude of auspicious qualities; the blameless one; the possessor of infinite great majesty;
the ocean of unsurpassed excellence, beauty, and affection; is the sovereign of all, while the self is subordinate to Him—[He alone is the object of devotion].

When contemplated as being free from all obstacles, it leads this very Self to the Supreme Brahman, which is the object of infinite and unsurpassed delight. Now, one might object: has it not been stated that the state of being the absolute end (*atyantaśeṣatā*) of the Self is itself infinite and unsurpassed bliss?

This is contrary to the consensus of all the world; for indeed, among all sentient beings, independence alone is seen to be most desired, while dependence is experienced as more painful. And there is a traditional teaching (smṛti):
Everything dependent on another is suffering; everything dependent on oneself is happiness.
For thus has servitude been described as the way of a dog; therefore, one should avoid it.
Thus [it is said]. This [notion] is the manifestation of the conceit of the body as the self among those who have not realized the nature of the self as distinct from the body.
For indeed, the body—being a physical aggregate that serves as the locus for qualities such as the genus "humanity" (manuṣyatva)—is perceived as independent;
and it is precisely upon that [body] that transmigrating beings have the cognition "I am."
The perception of the human goal is exactly in accordance with whatever kind of self-identification one possesses.

For those whose self-identifications are established as being a lion, a tiger, a boar, a human, a yakṣa, a rākṣasa, a piśāca, a god, a dānava, a woman, or a man, their respective pleasures are likewise established;
and these are mutually contradictory.
Therefore, everything is integrated through the systematic arrangement of human goals corresponding to the conceit of self (ātmābhimāna).
However, the true nature of the Self is distinct from the bodies of gods and others, consisting solely of the form of knowledge;
and that [nature] has as its sole essence being subservient to another (the Supreme).
When there is the conceit of a self as it truly exists, the perception of the human goal (puruṣārtha) conforms precisely to that [conceit].

From the Smṛti statement, "The Self consists of knowledge and is stainless," its nature as being solely of the form of knowledge is established. Furthermore, from the qualities of the Śruti such as "Lord of the universe," its nature as being solely of the form of subservience to the Supreme Self is perceived.

Therefore, just like the conceit of self-identity with the bodies of lions, tigers, and so forth, the conceit of independence should also be understood as a form of erroneous knowledge of the Self produced by karma.
Consequently, the state of pleasure in objects distinct from the Supreme Person is produced solely by karma;
for this very reason, those pleasures are limited and unstable, whereas the state of being pleasure itself belongs to the Supreme Person alone by His own nature.
Therefore, that alone is stable and possesses limitless excellence, according to the Śruti: "Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman, Ānanda is Brahman; Truth, Knowledge, and the Infinite is Brahman.

The Blessed Parāśara has stated that for everything other than Brahman, there is an absence of inherent happiness in its own nature, and it is unstable because it is produced by karma: "O best of the twice-born, what are known as hell and heaven are indeed sin and merit."
Since a single object leads to suffering, to pleasure, to the arising of envy,
and to anger, how can an object possess an inherent nature?
How can there be the substantiality of an entity that possesses an absolute form such as pleasure or pain?
The meaning is that its absoluteness is what produces merit and demerit.
Thus, having established the state in which, with respect to many persons, there is pleasure for one and pain for another, [the author proceeds].
He says that [feeling] is not fixed even in a single person:
"That very same thing, having become pleasant, arises again for suffering;
that very same thing arises for anger and for serenity."
Therefore, there is nothing whose nature is exclusively suffering, nor anything whose nature is exclusively happiness.
Thus, the quality of being composed of both pleasure and pain in every entity is produced by karma, not by the intrinsic nature of the thing itself;
consequently, the meaning is that this [quality] disappears when karma is exhausted. (144)

As for the statement that "everything dependent on another is suffering," this was said because, for those other than the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa), there is an absence of the relationship of mutual subservience and predominance; thus, being subservient to anyone other than Him is indeed suffering. In the passage, "Service is called the dog's life," it is likewise stated that service to one who is not worthy of service is precisely the dog's life. And in the words, "He alone is to be constantly worshipped by all the stages of life (āśramas)," it is meant that the Supreme Person (puruṣottama) alone is to be served by all those who know the true nature of the Self.
As it was said by the Blessed One:
"And he who serves Me with unswerving yoga of devotion,
having transcended these qualities, is fit for becoming Brahman."

Thus, it has been stated that this very service in the form of devotion is designated by the word "knowledge" (*vedana*) in such passages as, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," "He who knows thus becomes immortal here," and "One who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself. Furthermore,
from the specific qualification in the text, "He is obtained by whomsoever He chooses," it is understood that the Lord is the one who is to be chosen (*varaṇīyatva*).
And he is most beloved who is to be chosen;
he in whom an infinite and unsurpassed love for the Blessed One arises is indeed the most beloved of the Blessed One.
Thus it was said by the Blessed One:
"For I am exceedingly dear to the knower, and he is dear to Me.
Therefore, it is knowledge that has attained the form of supreme devotion alone which, in reality, is the means for attaining the Blessed One.
As was stated by the Blessed Lord Dvaipāyana in the *Mokṣadharma*, which serves as a commentary on all the Upaniṣads:
His form does not stand within the range of vision; no one beholds him with the eye.
But here, one whose self is composed through devotion and fortitude perceives his true nature as pure consciousness.
The meaning is that one who has a self composed through steadfastness perceives, that is, realizes and attains, the Supreme Person through devotion (*bhakti*).
This is because [the present verse] shares the same sense as the statement, "But by exclusive devotion He can be known.
Furthermore, since devotion is indeed a specific form of knowledge, everything is logically consistent. (145)
Since there exist those who are free from envy, who are capable of discerning the essential from the non-essential,
and who rely upon the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), this compendium of the meaning of the Vedas has been composed.
